title: Breaking Scale Separation in Metamaterials' homogenization: Interface-Inertia-Enhanced Relaxed Micromorphic Model
summary: Homogenized continuum models are widely used to describe wave propagation and band-gap behavior in mechanical metamaterials without explicitly resolving their microstructure. Their validity, however, typically relies on the classical separation of scales assumption, according to which the wavelength of the propagating disturbance is much larger than the characteristic size of the unit cell. In finite-size metamaterial samples and at higher frequencies, this assumption progressively breaks down, and the dynamic response becomes strongly influenced by the way the microstructure is truncated at the external boundaries. In this work we introduce a fundamentally new concept in the homogenized description of mechanical metamaterials: the inertial contribution of macroscopic interfaces. We show that different truncations of the same lattice generate boundaries with distinct mass distributions, which lead to measurable differences in the dynamic response of finite-sized specimens. To capture this complex mechanism in a homogenized framework, we extend the relaxed micromorphic model by introducing a kinetic surface energy defined on the boundary of the considered body. This generates an additional inertial term in the boundary conditions that can be seen as the homogenized counterpart of the interface inertia produced by the truncation of the microstructure. As a result, the homogenized model can now distinguish between finite-sized specimens that share identical bulk properties but differ only in the configuration of their interfaces. The proposed formulation preserves the variational structure of the relaxed micromorphic model while enabling the continuum to reproduce boundary-dependent responses observed in fully resolved simulations, particularly in frequency regimes ....... AI.tldr: This paper introduces a new concept for homogenized modeling of mechanical metamaterials: the inertial contribution of macroscopic interfaces. By extending the relaxed micromorphic model with a kinetic surface energy on boundaries, the homogenized continuum can capture boundary-dependent dynamic responses (e.g., band gaps, wave propagation) that arise from different truncations of the same lattice microstructure, overcoming the limitations of classical separation of scales.
AI.motivation: Classical homogenized continuum models rely on the separation of scales assumption, which breaks down in finite-size metamaterial samples and at higher frequencies. The dynamic response becomes strongly influenced by how the microstructure is truncated at external boundaries, but existing homogenized models cannot distinguish between specimens with identical bulk properties but different interface configurations.
AI.method: The authors extend the relaxed micromorphic model by introducing a kinetic surface energy defined on the boundary of the considered body. This generates an additional inertial term in the boundary conditions, which serves as the homogenized counterpart of interface inertia produced by microstructure truncation. The formulation preserves the variational structure of the relaxed micromorphic model.
AI.result: The homogenized model can now distinguish between finite-sized specimens that share identical bulk properties but differ only in their interface configurations. It reproduces boundary-dependent responses observed in fully resolved simulations, particularly in frequency regimes where classical assumptions fail.
AI.conclusion: Different truncations of the same lattice generate boundaries with distinct mass distributions leading to measurable differences in dynamic response. The proposed interface-inertia-extended relaxed micromorphic model successfully captures this mechanism, enabling more accurate homogenized descriptions of finite-size mechanical metamaterials.

title: Exact Total Variation Minimizers as Non-Oscillatory Limiters in High-Order Methods for Conservation Laws
summary: High-order numerical methods for conservation laws can generate spurious oscillations near discontinuities. We propose to suppress these oscillations by post-processing the numerical solution with a total variation (TV) denoising step that reduces the total variation of the nodal values. For a general analysis operator, the resulting discrete minimization problem need not satisfy the submodularity property that existing exact max-flow algorithms require, so we instead compute the TV minimizer exactly using a differential inclusion algorithm. In one dimension, the differential inclusion algorithm computes the TV minimizer in finitely many steps, requires no tuning of algorithmic parameters, and preserves the total mass. In two dimensions, we apply the 1D algorithm dimension by dimension. We test the method as a post-processing limiter for Fourier pseudospectral methods and a fifth-order finite difference scheme applied to scalar conservation laws, compressible Euler equations, and the two-dimensional incompressible Euler equations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a total variation (TV) denoising post-processing step to suppress spurious oscillations in high-order numerical methods for conservation laws. The TV minimizer is computed exactly using a differential inclusion algorithm that requires no parameter tuning, preserves total mass, and terminates in finitely many steps in 1D, extended dimension-by-dimension to 2D.
AI.motivation: High-order numerical methods for conservation laws produce spurious oscillations near discontinuities. Existing exact TV minimization approaches via max-flow algorithms require submodularity, which is not guaranteed for general analysis operators, motivating a different algorithmic approach.
AI.method: The authors post-process numerical solutions with a TV denoising step that reduces total variation of nodal values. Since the discrete minimization problem may lack submodularity (required by max-flow algorithms), they compute the TV minimizer exactly using a differential inclusion algorithm. In 1D this computes the minimizer in finitely many steps with no parameter tuning and mass conservation; in 2D the 1D algorithm is applied dimension by dimension.
AI.result: The method is tested as a post-processing limiter for Fourier pseudospectral methods and a fifth-order finite difference scheme applied to scalar conservation laws, compressible Euler equations, and 2D incompressible Euler equations.
AI.conclusion: The TV denoising approach with the differential inclusion algorithm provides an effective, parameter-free limiter that suppresses spurious oscillations across various high-order schemes and equation types.

title: Dynamical Low-Rank Filters for Data Assimilation
summary: We propose dynamical low-rank (DLR) type filters for data-assimilation problems based on stochastic differential equations (SDEs). In detail, first we derive a DLRA filter for minimizing jointly the mean and covariance error, as well as a strategy to efficiently include the relevant orthogonal directions. This last approach allows the main subspace to evolve also according to the observation operator. Those procedures naturally extend to a Kalman-Bucy type filter when dealing with linear drift, and to ensemble methods, too, resulting also suitable for problems described by nonlinear drift and possible non-Gaussian distribution. Moreover, we further propose a preliminary particle-type DLRA filter that shows potentiality in nonlinear settings. Numerical simulations show the efficacy of these procedures in relevant applications, opening up to further studies in these filtering directions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes dynamical low-rank (DLR) filters for data assimilation in SDE-based problems, including mean-covariance joint minimization filters, an efficient orthogonal direction inclusion strategy, natural extensions to Kalman-Bucy filters and ensemble methods, and a preliminary particle-type DLR filter for nonlinear settings.
AI.motivation: To address the computational challenges of data assimilation in high-dimensional stochastic systems by developing low-rank filtration approaches that reduce computational cost while maintaining accuracy.
AI.method: Derives dynamical low-rank approximation (DLRA) filters that minimize joint mean and covariance error, incorporates an efficient strategy for including relevant orthogonal directions allowing the main subspace to evolve according to the observation operator, extends these to Kalman-Bucy type filters for linear drift and ensemble methods for nonlinear drift/non-Gaussian distributions, and proposes a preliminary particle-type DLRA filter.
AI.result: Numerical simulations demonstrate efficacy of the proposed DLR filters in relevant applications, showing potential for nonlinear settings particularly with the particle-type approach.
AI.conclusion: The DLR type filters open up further studies in filtering directions for data assimilation problems, showing promise for both linear and nonlinear dynamical systems.

title: Comparison of a Parametric Physics-Informed Neural Network and a Tensorial Reduced-Order Model for the Shallow-Water Dam-Break Problem
summary: We develop two parametric data-driven reduced models: a physics-informed neural network (PINN) and a non-intrusive tensorial reduced-order model (TROM), and apply both approaches to the parametrized one-dimensional shallow-water dam-break problem. Both reduced models do not require time integration and learn a direct solution map from space, time, and dam-break parameters to the physical state. We present a detailed comparison for out-of-sample and extrapolated parameter values. In addition, we demonstrate that it is essential to introduce shock-aware collocation to improve the robustness of the PINN model.

AI.tldr: This paper develops and compares two parametric data-driven reduced models (PINN and TROM) for the 1D shallow-water dam-break problem, both learning a direct map from space, time, and parameters to the physical state without time integration. It shows that shock-aware collocation is essential for PINN robustness and provides detailed comparisons for out-of-sample and extrapolated parameters.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to develop efficient reduced-order models that avoid time integration and directly learn solution maps for parametrized dam-break problems, while also addressing the challenge of handling shocks in data-driven approaches like PINNs.
AI.method: Two approaches are developed: (1) a physics-informed neural network (PINN) with shock-aware collocation to improve robustness, and (2) a non-intrusive tensorial reduced-order model (TROM). Both learn a direct mapping from space, time, and dam-break parameters to the physical state without requiring time integration.
AI.result: The paper provides a detailed comparison of PINN and TROM performance for out-of-sample and extrapolated parameter values, and demonstrates that shock-aware collocation significantly improves the robustness of the PINN model.
AI.conclusion: Shock-aware collocation is essential for robust PINN performance in dam-break problems, and both PINN and TROM serve as viable non-intrusive reduced models for this parametrized problem.

title: LoKI-GM: a global model framework for plasma chemistry studies
comment: Submitted to Plasma Sources Science and Technology
summary: Global (zero-dimensional or spatially averaged) models are widely employed to study complex chemistries in low-temperature plasmas (LTPs). By adopting a spatially average description of the plasma, they substantially reduce the computational cost while still providing reliable and detailed insight into the key processes taking place in the plasma. In their most general formulation, global models involve the coupled solution of a Boltzmann solver (to describe the electron kinetics) and a Chemistry solver (to describe the heavy-species kinetics). This paper presents a tutorial on the LisbOn Kinetics Global Model (LoKI-GM) framework, developed in MATLAB and available as open-source code. The framework couples the Boltzmann solver LoKI-B, which solves the space-independent form of the two-term electron Boltzmann equation for non-magnetised non-equilibrium LTPs, excited by DC/HF electric fields or time-dependent (non-oscillatory) electric fields, and the Chemistry solver LoKI-C, which solves the system of zero-dimensional rate balance equations for the main charged and neutral species in the plasma and at the surface, receiving as input the kinetic schemes for the gas/plasma/surface system under study. The inclusion of several transport models together with support for surface kinetics models are distinguishing features of LoKI-GM compared with other global chemistry models. We briefly present the formulation of LoKI-GM, including its numerical solution strategy, input/output parameters, and calculation workflow for both active discharges and afterglow plasmas. The main differences with respect to existing global models are highlighted, and the flexibility of the code for plasma chemistry studies is demonstrated through representative simulation results obtained across a range of gas discharge configurations and operating conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a tutorial on LoKI-GM, an open-source MATLAB framework that couples two solvers—LoKI-B (a two-term Boltzmann solver for electron kinetics) and LoKI-C (a zero-dimensional chemistry solver for heavy-species kinetics)—to enable global modeling of complex chemistries in low-temperature plasmas, with support for multiple transport models and surface kinetics.
AI.motivation: Global (zero-dimensional) models are widely used to study complex low-temperature plasma chemistries because they significantly reduce computational cost while providing reliable insight into key plasma processes. The paper aims to present a tutorial and introduce the LoKI-GM framework as a flexible, open-source tool for the community.
AI.method: LoKI-GM couples LoKI-B, which solves the space-independent two-term electron Boltzmann equation for non-magnetised non-equilibrium LTPs under DC/HF or time-dependent electric fields, with LoKI-C, which solves zero-dimensional rate balance equations for charged and neutral species in the plasma and at surfaces. It incorporates several transport models and supports surface kinetics models, with workflows for both active discharges and afterglow plasmas.
AI.result: The framework's formulation, numerical solution strategy, input/output parameters, and calculation workflow are presented. Representative simulation results across various gas discharge configurations and operating conditions demonstrate the flexibility and capabilities of the code for plasma chemistry studies.
AI.conclusion: LoKI-GM is a distinguishing open-source global model framework due to its inclusion of multiple transport models and surface kinetics support, making it a flexible and valuable tool for plasma chemistry studies compared to existing global models.

title: Semilinear Elliptic Systems with Nonlocal Homogeneous Critical Nonlinearities
summary: This paper concerns a variational system of nonlinear elliptic equations that generalizes the classical Brezis-Nirenberg problem. In addition to considering vector-valued unknown functions in place of scalar-valued unknown functions, the problem under consideration generalizes the Brezis-Nirenberg problem in two directions. First, the nonlinearity is the sum of two homogeneous functions of suitable homogeneity degrees. Second, the Sobolev-critical term in the nonlinearity is nonlocal. We establish conditions under which a nontrivial solution to the system under consideration is guaranteed to exist and conditions under which the system under consideration admits only the trivial solution.

AI.tldr: The paper studies a variational system of nonlinear elliptic equations generalizing the Brezis-Nirenberg problem in three ways: vector-valued unknowns, nonlinearities that are sums of two homogeneous functions of different homogeneity degrees, and a nonlocal Sobolev-critical term. It establishes conditions guaranteeing both the existence of nontrivial solutions and conditions under which only the trivial solution exists.
AI.motivation: The classical Brezis-Nirenberg problem is a foundational result in nonlinear elliptic PDE theory, and generalizing it to vector-valued unknown functions, combined homogeneity structures, and nonlocal critical terms broadens the applicable framework for studying nonlinear elliptic systems with Sobolev-critical nonlinearities.
AI.method: The paper employs variational methods to analyze the system. It establishes existence conditions for nontrivial solutions and derives conditions under which the system admits only the trivial solution, likely using critical point theory and energy functional analysis tailored to the nonlocal critical term and the sum of homogeneous nonlinearities.
AI.result: The paper provides explicit conditions under which a nontrivial solution to the generalized system is guaranteed to exist, as well as complementary conditions under which the system admits only the trivial solution.
AI.conclusion: The work extends the Brezis-Nirenberg problem to a broader class of nonlinear elliptic systems with nonlocal critical exponents, offering a complete characterization (existence vs. non-existence of nontrivial solutions) depending on the parameters of the problem.

title: Performance Benchmarking: Software for the Density Matrix Renormalization Group
summary: The performance of scientific software often determines the scale of problems that can be solved in practice. As multiple implementations of the same algorithm emerge, systematic evaluation is needed to compare their strengths and limitations. The density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) algorithm, widely used to study quantum systems, has over 50 software implementations. These implementations vary in multiple aspects that can strongly affect performance. However, despite the need, performance evaluations of these implementations are scarce and lack a consistent standard; many existing evaluations are either too incomplete to enable meaningful comparisons or focus on objectives other than direct performance comparisons, thereby limiting understanding of how the implementations compare. Here, we present a performance-oriented benchmarking framework to facilitate meaningful comparisons of DMRG implementations, and we apply it to quantify the performance of eight implementations, highlighting similarities and differences among them. Furthermore, we examine multiple parameter settings, optimization strategies, and implementation-specific features to demonstrate how parameter configuration can affect performance and how systematic evaluation can reveal non-obvious trade-offs. The results show significant performance differences, up to two orders of magnitude in some cases, not only between different implementations when aligning parameters, but also within the same implementation when comparing different parameter configurations. Hence, our results demonstrate the significant value and insight that can be gained from conducting rigorous performance evaluations. Using our results and framework as a starting point, more rigorous benchmarking will ultimately help users and developers make informed decisions and support future development efforts to build better, more efficient software.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a performance-oriented benchmarking framework for Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) software implementations, applied to eight implementations to quantify performance differences. Results show up to two orders of magnitude performance variation both across implementations (with aligned parameters) and within implementations (across parameter configurations), demonstrating the value of rigorous systematic evaluation.
AI.motivation: With over 50 DMRG software implementations existing, there is a critical need for systematic, consistent performance evaluation. However, existing evaluations are scarce, lack standardization, are often incomplete, or focus on objectives other than direct performance comparison, limiting understanding of how implementations compare.
AI.method: The authors develop a performance-oriented benchmarking framework designed to enable meaningful comparisons of DMRG implementations. They apply it to eight implementations, examining multiple parameter settings, optimization strategies, and implementation-specific features to quantify performance and reveal trade-offs.
AI.result: The framework reveals significant performance differences, up to two orders of magnitude, both between different implementations (when parameters are aligned) and within the same implementation (across parameter configurations). Systematic evaluation exposes non-obvious trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: Rigorous performance benchmarking provides substantial value and insight for DMRG software. The framework and results serve as a foundation for more rigorous benchmarking that will help users and developers make informed decisions and support future development of more efficient software.

title: Dynamical Low-Rank Smoothing
summary: Computational costs often make smoothing procedures prohibitive for high-dimensional data assimilation problems. To address this challenge, we propose a dynamical low-rank approximation (DLRA) methodology for smoothing concerning frameworks based on stochastic differential equations. We extend the previously developed joint mean-and-covariance optimization (JMCO) filtering setting to derive a reduced-order smoother via the Rauch--Tung--Striebel recursion and establish the corresponding Kalman--Bucy smoothing for affine drift dynamics. The resulting algorithms retain the adaptive nature of DLRA while significantly reducing the computational time and storage of the whole smoothing procedure.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a dynamical low-rank approximation (DLRA) methodology for smoothing in high-dimensional data assimilation problems based on stochastic differential equations, extending the joint mean-and-covariance optimization (JMCO) filtering framework to derive a reduced-order smoother via Rauch-Tung-Striebel recursion and Kalman-Bucy smoothing for affine drift dynamics.
AI.motivation: High-dimensional data assimilation smoothing procedures are often computationally prohibitive due to the cost of computing full covariance matrices. There is a need for reduced-order approaches that maintain accuracy while reducing computational burden.
AI.method: The authors extend the joint mean-and-covariance optimization (JMCO) filtering framework to the smoothing context, deriving a reduced-order smoother using the Rauch-Tung-Striebel recursion and establishing Kalman-Bucy smoothing for affine drift dynamics, all within a dynamical low-rank approximation (DLRA) framework.
AI.result: The resulting algorithms retain the adaptive nature of DLRA while significantly reducing both computational time and storage requirements for the entire smoothing procedure.
AI.conclusion: The DLRA-based smoothing framework provides an efficient and practical solution for high-dimensional data assimilation problems where traditional smoothing methods are computationally infeasible.

title: Coaxial Gyromagnetic Nonlinear Transmission Line with a Slow-Wave Structure: 2D/3D FDTD Modeling
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Plasma Science (Manuscript ID: TPS18901). Materials of this paper were presented as a poster report "2D/3D FDTD Modeling of Coaxial Waveguide with Magnetized Nonlinear Ferrite and Slow-Wave Structure" at the XXXII International Workshop on Optical Wave & Waveguide Theory and Numerical Modelling, 8-10 April 2026, Lausanne, Switzerland (https://owtnm26.epfl.ch/)
summary: A coaxial gyromagnetic nonlinear transmission line (GNLTL) enables pulse-front compression and oscillation packet generation in the 0.3-10 GHz range. Numerical modeling of such systems typically employs a 2D axially symmetric FDTD scheme coupled with the parallel solution of full non-linearized Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equations. Previous studies have shown that using an insulating dielectric with a permittivity $ε$>60 enables the generation of long-lasting oscillations via a Cherenkov-like effect. However, practical implementation is limited due to the severe high-frequency losses inherent in materials with such extreme permittivity, like water. To overcome this limitation and enhance performance, we propose a novel design utilizing a spiral central conductor to mimic a high-permittivity environment, with the ferrite placed inside the spiral. Due to the loss of axial symmetry, the FDTD model was extended to 3D coordinates. Simulations confirm that the spiral conductor configuration generates a prolonged oscillation packet similar to that of a high-permittivity dielectric waveguide, but with significantly reduced losses and improved energy transfer efficiency.

AI.tldr: A 3D FDTD simulation study demonstrates that a spiral central conductor design in a coaxial gyromagnetic nonlinear transmission line can replace high-permittivity dielectrics, achieving prolonged oscillation packet generation with reduced losses and improved energy efficiency.
AI.motivation: Previous designs using insulating dielectrics with permittivity >60 enabled long-lasting oscillations via a Cherenkov-like effect, but practical implementation is hindered by severe high-frequency losses in such extreme-permittivity materials like water.
AI.method: A novel spiral central conductor design mimics a high-permittivity environment with the ferrite placed inside the spiral, requiring extension of the FDTD model from 2D axially symmetric to full 3D coordinates due to loss of axial symmetry.
AI.result: Simulations confirm the spiral conductor configuration generates a prolonged oscillation packet similar to that of a high-permittivity dielectric waveguide, but with significantly reduced losses and improved energy transfer efficiency in the 0.3-10 GHz range.
AI.conclusion: The spiral conductor approach offers a practical alternative to extreme-permittivity dielectrics for generating long-lasting oscillations in GNLTL systems, overcoming the loss limitations of previous designs.

title: Remarks on some quasi-linear fourth order parabolic equations arising in mathematical physics
summary: This note proves existence and uniqueness of strong solutions to a broad class of fourth-order quasi-linear parabolic equations in the class of Wiener spaces. It improves upon previous results in the literature, devoted to some special cases falling within the general framework developed here, in which uniqueness held true in a smaller class than the space where existence was proven. Gain of analyticity, as well as generalisations to higher-order equations and to propagation of higher regularities, are also discussed.

AI.tldr: This paper proves existence and uniqueness of strong solutions for a broad class of fourth-order quasi-linear parabolic equations in Wiener spaces, improving on prior results that only established uniqueness in a smaller class than existence.
AI.motivation: Previous literature only addressed special cases of fourth-order quasi-linear parabolic equations, and crucially, uniqueness was proven in a smaller class than where existence was established—leaving a gap. This work aims to close that gap by developing a general framework that covers these special cases while ensuring uniqueness holds in the same full class.
AI.method: The paper develops a general framework in Wiener spaces that unifies previously studied special cases, proving existence and uniqueness of strong solutions for the broad class of fourth-order quasi-linear parabolic equations. It also extends the analysis to discuss analyticity gain, higher-order equations, and propagation of higher regularities.
AI.result: The paper establishes existence and uniqueness of strong solutions in the full solution class (improving on prior work where uniqueness held in a smaller class), and provides generalizations to higher-order equations and propagation of higher regularities, along with a discussion of analyticity gain.
AI.conclusion: The general framework successfully resolves the uniqueness gap present in prior literature and extends the theory to broader settings including higher-order equations and higher regularity propagation.

title: Fast and Accurate Foundation Models for Equivariant Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
summary: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have emerged as a transformative tool for computational materials science and chemistry, with universal potentials trained on large and diverse datasets now routinely deployed as 'foundation models' for downstream fine-tuning in targeted chemical spaces. Many scientific applications of the resulting models, such as molecular dynamics (MD), require high inference and training speeds as well as accuracy. In this work, we examine the limits of equivariant MLIPs, which directly encode physical symmetries in model architectures, to achieve these competing targets -- particularly in the regime of extremely large datasets where data efficiency is less critical. We show how this trade-off can be addressed, and present a family of foundation potentials in the NequIP and Allegro equivariant MLIP architectures which achieve leading inference speeds and strong scalability as well as excellent accuracies across a range of community benchmarks -- spanning materials discovery, thermal conductivity prediction, and near-equilibrium mechanical and thermodynamic properties. Accelerations implemented within the NequIP infrastructure now permit training of high-accuracy foundation potentials on ultra-large datasets with dramatically reduced computational cost. Alongside, we show that efforts to improve model accuracy for materials discovery should focus on dataset diversity and improved, consistent descriptions of transition metal compound energy surfaces.

AI.tldr: This paper presents equivariant machine-learned interatomic potentials (NequIP/Allegro architectures) as foundation models that achieve leading inference speeds, strong scalability, and excellent accuracy across materials benchmarks, while addressing the trade-off between accuracy and speed at the ultra-large dataset scale.
AI.motivation: Universal MLIPs are increasingly used as foundation models for downstream fine-tuning, but many scientific applications (e.g., MD) require high inference/training speeds alongside accuracy. The authors aim to examine whether equivariant MLIP architectures can achieve these competing targets, particularly in the ultra-large dataset regime where data efficiency matters less.
AI.method: The authors implement accelerations within the NequIP infrastructure and construct a family of foundation potentials based on NequIP and Allegro equivariant architectures, optimizing for inference speed, scalability, and accuracy. They evaluate these models across diverse community benchmarks including materials discovery, thermal conductivity prediction, and near-equilibrium mechanical/thermodynamic properties.
AI.result: The equivariant foundation potentials achieve leading inference speeds, strong scalability, and excellent accuracy across benchmarks. Training of high-accuracy foundation potentials on ultra-large datasets is enabled with dramatically reduced computational cost. Additionally, the analysis reveals that improving model accuracy for materials discovery should prioritize dataset diversity and consistent descriptions of transition metal compound energy surfaces.
AI.conclusion: Equivariant MLIPs can successfully balance accuracy and speed as foundation potentials at scale, and future accuracy improvements for materials discovery should be driven by dataset quality/diversity rather than purely architectural changes.

title: Residual-Driven Lifting Identification for Nonlinear-Manifold Reduced-Order Models of Parametrized Linear PDEs
summary: We introduce a residual-driven procedure for training nonlinear-manifold reduced-order models for parametrized linear partial differential equations that, given prescribed latent and lifting spaces, identifies the nonlinear lifting without high-fidelity solution snapshots. The approximation is represented by a low-dimensional latent coordinate together with a nonlinear lifting into a richer reduced space. Rather than fitting the lifting to snapshot data, we determine it by minimizing a computable residual-based upper bound for the state error. For affinely parametrized operators, the resulting training objective admits an efficient offline--online decomposition, and the lifting update reduces to a sequence of low-dimensional weighted least-squares problems. Numerical evaluations on an advection--diffusion problem and a plane-strain elasticity benchmark show that the proposed approach substantially improves accuracy over linear subspaces. The resulting nonlinear models achieve accuracy comparable to snapshot-driven nonlinear-manifold training while avoiding high-fidelity snapshots in the lifting-identification stage.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a residual-driven training method for nonlinear-manifold reduced-order models (ROMs) for parametrized linear PDEs. It identifies nonlinear liftings by minimizing a computable residual-based error bound, without requiring high-fidelity solution snapshots, and demonstrates improved accuracy over linear subspaces on advection-diffusion and elasticity benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional nonlinear-manifold ROMs require high-fidelity solution snapshots to train the nonlinear lifting, which is costly and limits applicability. The authors aim to develop a snapshot-free training approach that can still achieve high accuracy for parametrized linear PDEs.
AI.method: The proposed procedure works as follows: (1) prescribe latent and lifting spaces for the ROM; (2) represent the approximation via a low-dimensional latent coordinate plus a nonlinear lifting into a richer reduced space; (3) instead of fitting the lifting to snapshot data, minimize a computable residual-based upper bound for the state error; (4) for affinely parametrized operators, the training objective admits an efficient offline-online decomposition; (5) the lifting update reduces to a sequence of low-dimensional weighted least-squares problems.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on an advection-diffusion problem and a plane-strain elasticity benchmark show the proposed approach substantially improves accuracy over linear subspaces. The nonlinear models achieve accuracy comparable to snapshot-driven nonlinear-manifold training while avoiding high-fidelity snapshots in the lifting-identification stage.
AI.conclusion: Residual-driven training is a viable, snapshot-free alternative for identifying nonlinear liftings in reduced-order models for parametrized linear PDEs, achieving accuracy competitive with snapshot-driven approaches while reducing data requirements.

title: The Second Quadratic Invariant of Astrophysical Gyrokinetics
summary: We show that gyrokinetics in a spatially uniform equilibrium (or `astrophysical gyrokinetics') possesses a previously unknown quadratic invariant, which we call the gyrokinetic helicity. We derive the limiting forms of the gyrokinetic helicity in five subsidiary expansions of astrophysical gyrokinetics: the isothermal electron fluid (ITEF) approximation, kinetic reduced magnetohydrodynamics (KRMHD), electron reduced magnetohydrodynamics (ERMHD), finite-Larmor-radius magnetohydrodynamics (FLR-MHD), and the kinetic reduced electron heating model~(KREHM). We subdivide the real part of the gyrokinetic helicity into `magnetofluid' and `phase-space' components, which are separately conserved in KRMHD, ERMHD, and FLR-MHD (in which there is no phase-space helicity). The magnetofluid helicity is equivalent to the Alfvénic part of the cross helicity in KRMHD, the magnetic helicity in~ERMHD, and the generalized helicity in FLR-MHD and~KREHM. We derive an analytic expression for the rate at which magnetofluid helicity is converted into phase-space helicity at length scales comparable to the proton gyroradius in the ITEF approximation. We also explain how this conversion circumvents the helicity barrier and enhances turbulent heating in coronal holes and the near-Sun solar wind.

AI.tldr: This paper discovers a new quadratic invariant called gyrokinetic helicity in astrophysical gyrokinetics (spatially uniform equilibrium). The authors derive its limiting forms in five subsidiary approximations (ITEF, KRMHD, ERMHD, FLR-MHD, KREHM), split it into magnetofluid and phase-space components, and show how helicity is converted between these components at proton gyroradius scales, which explains how the helicity barrier is circumvented and turbulent heating is enhanced in coronal holes and the near-Sun solar wind.
AI.motivation: To identify a previously unknown conserved quantity (gyrokinetic helicity) in astrophysical gyrokinetics and understand how helicity dynamics at kinetic scales affect turbulent heating and the helicity barrier in space plasmas.
AI.method: The authors derive the gyrokinetic helicity invariant in astrophysical gyrokinetics and its limiting forms in five subsidiary expansions. They decompose the helicity into magnetofluid and phase-space components, analyze their conservation properties in various approximations, and derive an analytic expression for the conversion rate between these components at proton gyroradius scales.
AI.result: The gyrokinetic helicity reduces to Alfvénic cross helicity in KRMHD, magnetic helicity in ERMHD, and generalized helicity in FLR-MHD and KREHM. The magnetofluid and phase-space components are separately conserved in KRMHD, ERMHD, and FLR-MHD. An analytic expression for magnetofluid-to-phase-space helicity conversion rate at proton gyroradius scales is derived, showing how this conversion circumvents the helicity barrier.
AI.conclusion: The gyrokinetic helicity is a fundamental invariant of astrophysical gyrokinetics that unifies various known helicity invariants across different approximations, and the conversion of magnetofluid to phase-space helicity at kinetic scales plays a key role in enhancing turbulent heating by getting around the helicity barrier in coronal holes and the near-Sun solar wind.

title: Rigorous justification of the hydrostatic-incompressible approximation for weakly stratified isothermal flow
summary: We consider the limit of small Mach number and small vertical-to-horizontal aspect ratio for the isothermal compressible Navier-Stokes system. In addition, we consider the scale in which the stratification is weak. Owing to the anisotropic nature of the problem, the dynamics exhibit a three-wave separation phenomenon, consistent of a slow wave, a fast horizontal acoustic wave, and an even faster vertical acoustic wave. These three waves, unfortunately, are not mutually orthogonal, and the corresponding projections are parametrized by the small parameter, which significantly complicates the nonlinear analysis. Without any restriction on the size of the initial waves, we establish the uniform existence and uniqueness of solutions to the compressible Navier-Stokes system for any fixed small parameter, by carefully analyzing the evolutions of both the energy and the acoustic waves. Moreover, we prove that, as the small parameter tends to zero, the solutions converge to that of the incompressible primitive equations governing atmospheric and oceanic flows.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the low Mach number and small aspect ratio limit of the isothermal compressible Navier-Stokes system with weak stratification. The authors identify a three-wave separation phenomenon (slow wave, fast horizontal acoustic wave, faster vertical acoustic wave) and prove uniform existence/uniqueness of solutions without restrictions on initial wave sizes, showing convergence to the incompressible primitive equations as the small parameter tends to zero.
AI.motivation: To rigorously understand the mathematical derivation of the incompressible primitive equations (which govern atmospheric and oceanic flows) from the compressible Navier-Stokes system under physically relevant scaling limits—specifically, small Mach number, small aspect ratio, and weak stratification simultaneously.
AI.method: The authors consider the coupled singular limit of small Mach number and small vertical-to-horizontal aspect ratio with weak stratification. They identify a three-wave separation structure (slow, fast horizontal acoustic, and faster vertical acoustic waves) where the non-orthogonality of these waves complicates the nonlinear analysis. They carefully track the evolutions of both energy and acoustic waves to establish uniform estimates without imposing size restrictions on initial waves.
AI.result: The paper establishes uniform existence and uniqueness of solutions to the compressible Navier-Stokes system for any fixed small parameter, without restrictions on the size of initial waves. Furthermore, it proves convergence of these solutions to the incompressible primitive equations as the small parameter tends to zero.
AI.conclusion: The anisotropic limit provides a rigorous justification of the incompressible primitive equations from the compressible Navier-Stokes system, overcoming the significant complication arising from the lack of mutual orthogonality among the three separated waves.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for 2D Plane Wave Scattering in Arbitrary Dielectric Structures
summary: In this paper, we introduce a meshless physics-informed neural network based computational framework for solving two-dimensional electromagnetic wave scattering in inhomogeneous media. The framework embeds frequency-domain Maxwell equations and radiation boundary conditions directly into the neural network loss function, enabling accurate prediction of scattered fields for both transverse magnetic (TM) and transverse electric (TE) polarizations across various dielectric configurations. Application of the method to single-cylinder, concentric multilayer cylindrical shells, three arbitrarily arranged cylinders, and composite irregular structures demonstrates that for the TM polarization, all relative $L^{2}$ errors mostly remain at particularly low levels of $\le0.1$. For the TE polarization, sharp variations of the dielectric properties of scatterers lead to singularities in the governing equations, which result in decreased accuracy of the method. This challenge is overcome by introducing at dielectric boundaries a hyperbolic-tangent smoothing function. This procedure significantly improves the accuracy of the method, with the corresponding results closely matching the predictions of the finite-difference time-domain method. This framework exhibits stable convergence behavior across all of the investigated configurations, thus confirming its robustness and scalability to complex electromagnetic scattering problems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a meshless physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework for solving 2D electromagnetic wave scattering in inhomogeneous media, embedding Maxwell's equations and radiation boundary conditions directly into the loss function. The method achieves low relative L2 errors (<0.1) for TM polarization across various geometries, while TE polarization accuracy is improved via a hyperbolic-tangent smoothing function at dielectric boundaries.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to develop a computational framework that overcomes limitations of traditional mesh-based numerical methods (such as finite-difference time-domain) for electromagnetic wave scattering problems in inhomogeneous media, particularly to handle complex and irregular geometries without requiring mesh generation.
AI.method: A meshless PINN framework is introduced where frequency-domain Maxwell equations and radiation boundary conditions are embedded directly into the neural network loss function. For TE polarization accuracy issues caused by sharp dielectric property variations, a hyperbolic-tangent smoothing function is applied at dielectric boundaries.
AI.result: The method was tested on single-cylinder, concentric multilayer cylindrical shells, three arbitrarily arranged cylinders, and composite irregular structures. TM polarization achieved relative L2 errors mostly at or below 0.1. TE polarization, after applying the hyperbolic-tangent smoothing, closely matched finite-difference time-domain predictions with significantly improved accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The proposed PINN framework exhibits stable convergence behavior across all investigated configurations, confirming its robustness and scalability for complex electromagnetic scattering problems, making it a viable meshless alternative to traditional numerical methods.

title: Scalable Graph Coreset Selection via Greedy Sampling
summary: Sampling representative nodes from large graphs is fundamental to graph signal processing and network analysis, yet existing methods require access to the full graph Laplacian, making them impractical at scale. We propose a simple and effective column-selective graph sampling algorithm based on a minimum inner product greedy selection rule. At each iteration, the algorithm accesses only a small random subset of Laplacian columns, requiring no eigendecomposition or global graph traversal, making it well-suited for large-scale graphs where the full Laplacian cannot be stored in memory. We analyze the algorithm under the stochastic block model and show that, when the degree distribution is balanced across nodes, the algorithm achieves sampling proportional to cluster size, and that the resulting mean estimate is controlled for band-limited graph signals in the Paley-Wiener space, with the error decaying as inter-cluster connectivity weakens. Numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world data validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a column-selective graph sampling algorithm using a minimum inner product greedy selection rule that accesses only small random subsets of Laplacian columns, avoiding eigendecomposition and full graph traversal. It is analyzed under the stochastic block model and validated on synthetic and real-world data.
AI.motivation: Existing graph sampling methods require access to the full graph Laplacian, making them impractical for large-scale graphs that cannot be stored in memory.
AI.method: A column-selective graph sampling algorithm based on a minimum inner product greedy selection rule. At each iteration, it accesses only a small random subset of Laplacian columns, requiring no eigendecomposition or global graph traversal.
AI.result: Under the stochastic block model with balanced degree distribution, the algorithm achieves sampling proportional to cluster size, and the mean estimate error is controlled for band-limited graph signals in the Paley-Wiener space, decaying as inter-cluster connectivity weakens. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world data validate effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method is a simple, scalable, and effective approach for sampling representative nodes from large graphs without the need for full Laplacian storage.

title: Effect of confinement anisotropy on particle transport and structural relaxation of finite dust clusters in complex plasma
summary: A finite dusty plasma cluster of charged microparticles confined in an anisotropic potential well is investigated experimentally and through Langevin dynamics simulations. As the confinement anisotropy is increased, the cluster undergoes a structural transition from near isotropic concentric shells to a linear chain configuration. The spatiotemporal modes of the cluster are analyzed by using Singular Value Decomposition. At weaker confinement anisotropies, two modes are dominant. Mode 1, corresponding to a breathing-type oscillation of the cluster, and mode 2, representing an azimuthal rotational motion of the cluster, together carry around 99$\%$ of the signal energy. With increasing anisotropy, the dominance of mode 2 decreases and that of mode 1 increases. This mode restructuring is accompanied by an increasingly non-Gaussian particle displacement statistics as evidenced by positive values of the Non-Gaussian Parameter maintained over an extended time duration. Simultaneously, the increasing dominance of mode 1 and suppression of mode 2 is accompanied by a significant slowing down of structural relaxation, with the cluster eventually exhibiting signatures of structural arrest. At weaker anisotropy, the experimentally measured dynamical quantities are very sensitive to the initial conditions which account for the discrepancy between the experiment and initial condition averaged simulation results for these observables. This study offers insight into the mechanisms underlying anomalous transport and structural relaxation in anisotropically confined many-body systems.

AI.tldr: A dusty plasma cluster confined in an anisotropic potential well is studied experimentally and via Langevin simulations. As anisotropy increases, the cluster transitions from concentric shells to a linear chain, with mode restructuring (breathing vs. rotational modes), increasingly non-Gaussian dynamics, slowing structural relaxation, and eventual structural arrest.
AI.motivation: To understand the mechanisms underlying anomalous transport and structural relaxation in anisotropically confined many-body systems, particularly how confinement anisotropy affects the structural and dynamical properties of finite particle clusters.
AI.method: Experimental investigation of charged microparticles in an anisotropic potential well combined with Langevin dynamics simulations. Spatiotemporal modes were analyzed using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), and particle displacement statistics were characterized via the Non-Gaussian Parameter.
AI.result: At weak anisotropy, two dominant modes carry ~99% of signal energy: mode 1 (breathing-type oscillation) and mode 2 (azimuthal rotational motion). Increased anisotropy suppresses mode 2 while enhancing mode 1, leading to non-Gaussian displacement statistics, significant slowing of structural relaxation, and signatures of structural arrest. Discrepancies between experiment and simulation at weak anisotropy are attributed to sensitivity to initial conditions.
AI.conclusion: Anisotropic confinement drives a structural transition from shells to chains, accompanied by mode restructuring and dynamical slowing toward structural arrest, offering insight into anomalous transport in confined many-body systems.

title: On the upper bound for the vorticity growth of bi-rotational Euler flows without swirl
summary: For $d\geq 4$, we consider incompressible Euler flows in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with bi-rotational symmetry and without swirl. Our first result gives the local wellposedness of the Yudovich-type solution. The second result provides global wellposedness up to $d\leq 6$. In particular, it shows that the rate of growth of the vorticity maximum coincides with the rate from axisymmetric flows without swirl, which was obtained in the paper by the second author and Jeong (Arch. Ration. Mech. Anal. 249(3):32, 2025) and Shao--Wei--Zhang (Acta Math. Sin. (Engl. Ser.), 42(3):663-679, 2026).

AI.tldr: This paper studies incompressible Euler flows in R^d (d≥4) with bi-rotational symmetry and no swirl. It establishes local wellposedness of Yudovich-type solutions and global wellposedness for d≤6, showing the vorticity maximum growth rate matches that of axisymmetric flows without swirl.
AI.motivation: To extend wellposedness results for Euler equations beyond the classical axisymmetric case to bi-rotational symmetric flows, which are higher-dimensional analogues that preserve certain rotational symmetries in R^d.
AI.method: The paper considers incompressible Euler flows in R^d with bi-rotational symmetry and without swirl, and analyzes Yudovich-type solutions for local wellposedness. For global wellposedness up to d≤6, it tracks the growth rate of the vorticity maximum and compares it with known results for axisymmetric flows without swirl.
AI.result: Local wellposedness of Yudovich-type solutions is established. Global wellposedness is proven up to d≤6, and the vorticity maximum growth rate coincides with that of axisymmetric flows without swirl from prior works by the second author with Jeong, and by Shao-Wei-Zhang.
AI.conclusion: Bi-rotational symmetric Euler flows share the same quantitative behavior (vorticity growth rate) as axisymmetric flows without swirl, providing a unified picture of wellposedness for these symmetric higher-dimensional Euler flows.

title: A sub-grid-scale model for polydisperse bubbly flows with heat and mass transfer
summary: Ensemble-averaged models of polydisperse bubbly flows require statistics of the evolving bubble population. Prior quadrature-based moment formulations close bubble pressure with a polytropic relation that omits heat and mass transfer at the bubble wall. We formulate constant-transfer equations for bubble pressure and vapor mass within a conditional hyperbolic quadrature method. Second-order conditional inversion produces four joint radius--radial-velocity nodes per equilibrium-radius bin. Bubble pressure and vapor mass are advanced at each node. The node values close the ensemble-averaged flow equations without adding mixed pressure or vapor-mass moments to the transported moment set. The model is implemented in MFC. Monte Carlo calculations verify the evolution of quadrature nodes and the mean bubble variables for a harmonically forced population. Bubble-screen calculations quantify closure error as the equilibrium radius is discretized and the initial distributions vary. The constant-transfer calculation does not exhibit the high-frequency pressure oscillations observed with the polytropic closure under the conditions considered. 3D bubble-screen calculations give a 1.5% relative root-mean-square error between the Euler--Euler center pressure and the mean of 40 volume-averaged Euler--Lagrange realizations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a conditional hyperbolic quadrature method for polydisperse bubbly flows that closes bubble pressure and vapor mass using constant-transfer equations, avoiding the polytropic approximation's omission of heat/mass transfer. The method advances bubble pressure and vapor mass at each quadrature node without adding mixed moments, showing improved stability (no high-frequency oscillations) and accuracy (1.5% RMS error vs. Euler-Lagrange reference).
AI.motivation: Ensemble-averaged models of polydisperse bubbly flows require accurate statistics of the evolving bubble population. Prior quadrature-based moment formulations close bubble pressure with a polytropic relation that omits heat and mass transfer at the bubble wall, which is a significant physical limitation for realistic bubbly flows.
AI.method: The authors formulate constant-transfer equations for bubble pressure and vapor mass within a conditional hyperbolic quadrature method. Second-order conditional inversion produces four joint radius-radial-velocity nodes per equilibrium-radius bin, where bubble pressure and vapor mass are advanced at each node. These node values close the ensemble-averaged flow equations without adding mixed pressure or vapor-mass moments to the transported moment set. The model is implemented in the MFC (Multi-component Flow Code) framework.
AI.result: Monte Carlo calculations verify the evolution of quadrature nodes and mean bubble variables for harmonically forced populations. Bubble-screen calculations quantify closure error as equilibrium radius is discretized and initial distributions vary. The constant-transfer calculation avoids high-frequency pressure oscillations seen with polytropic closure. 3D bubble-screen calculations yield 1.5% relative root-mean-square error between the Euler-Euler center pressure and the mean of 40 volume-averaged Euler-Lagrange realizations.
AI.conclusion: The constant-transfer conditional hyperbolic quadrature method provides an accurate and stable closure for polydisperse bubbly flows, overcoming limitations of the polytropic relation by incorporating heat and mass transfer effects at the bubble wall while maintaining computational efficiency in the moment set.

title: A novel sampling method for reconstruction of a moving point acoustic source in $\mathbb{R}^3$
summary: In this paper, we introduce a novel sampling method to recovering the trajectory of a moving point source in R^3, where both the spatial location and emission moment of the moving point source are unknown. Combining algebraic theory with geometric knowledge, we prove the uniqueness of the source location by using measured data from five observation points. Our sampling method constructs an indicator function based on the property that the residual of the time difference of arrival constraint formula vanishes at the true source location. It achieves the reconstruction of the spatial positions and emission moments of a moving point source only using data from five observation points and their corresponding arrival times. The algorithm not only reduces the required number of observation points, but also improves computational efficiency, stability, and noise resistance. Numerical experiments verify the effectiveness of the method.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a novel sampling method for reconstructing the trajectory of a moving point source in R^3, where both spatial location and emission moment are unknown, using data from just five observation points. The method proves uniqueness of source location via algebraic-geometric theory and constructs an indicator function based on the residual of the TDOA constraint formula vanishing at the true location, improving computational efficiency, stability, and noise resistance.
AI.motivation: The problem of recovering the trajectory of a moving point source is challenging because both the spatial location and emission time are unknown. Traditional approaches require many observation points, which is inefficient and less practical. The authors aim to reduce the required number of observation points while maintaining accuracy and robustness.
AI.method: The method combines algebraic theory with geometric knowledge to prove the uniqueness of source location from five observation points. It constructs an indicator function based on the property that the residual of the time difference of arrival (TDOA) constraint formula vanishes at the true source location, enabling simultaneous reconstruction of spatial positions and emission moments through a sampling approach.
AI.result: The algorithm reduces the required number of observation points and improves computational efficiency, stability, and noise resistance. Numerical experiments confirm the effectiveness of the proposed method.
AI.conclusion: The proposed sampling method successfully reconstructs moving point source trajectories using only five observation points and their corresponding arrival times, offering a more efficient and robust alternative to existing approaches.

title: Electromagnetically Driven Thermal Dissipation Scaling in Plasma Centrifuges for Mass Separation
summary: Electromagnetically driven centrifuges (EMDCs) rotate fluids using the Lorentz force, but their separative performance is limited by thermal dissipation that is coupled to electromagnetic forcing. This follows because local centrifugal strength is proportional to λ=mV_θ^2/2k_B T, which compares directed kinetic energy that drives species separation to thermal energy that smooths concentration gradients and counteracts separation. In this work, we develop a reduced two-temperature magnetohydrodynamic model to determine how radial geometry, current density, and magnetic field strength control the coupled evolution of rotation and heating that dictates λ. The model is benchmarked against Ar and Ar/Kr experiments spanning current density up to 15 kA/m^2, magnetic field up to 0.57 T, feed pressures of 0.5-3 Torr, and annulus sizes of 1-5 cm. The results show that volumetric Lorentz forcing sustains higher λ and therefore greater local compositional shifts throughout a larger radial portion of the fluid volume than wall-bounded shear centrifuges, despite lower peak λ. Simulations of a 40Ar/36Ar isotopic mixture demonstrate that, when electromagnetic force and geometry are jointly optimized, EMDCs can exceed the separative performance of shear-driven centrifuges operating near material speed limits, for lower area-averaged values of λ. These results challenge assertions that viscous dissipation constrains weakly ionized plasma centrifuges to λ<1, and indicate that enhanced radial mass separation can be achieved by increasing the radial distribution of λ rather than maximizing its peak or area-averaged value.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a reduced two-temperature magnetohydrodynamic model to analyze electromagnetically driven centrifuges (EMDCs), showing that volumetric Lorentz forcing sustains higher separative performance (λ) across a larger radial portion of the fluid than wall-bounded shear centrifuges, despite lower peak λ. Simulations demonstrate that with joint optimization of electromagnetic force and geometry, EMDCs can exceed the separative performance of shear-driven centrifuges, challenging prior assertions that viscous dissipation limits weakly ionized plasma centrifuges to λ<1.
AI.motivation: EMDCs rotate fluids using the Lorentz force but their separative performance is limited by thermal dissipation coupled to electromagnetic forcing. Previous work suggested viscous dissipation constrains weakly ionized plasma centrifuges to λ<1, and the authors aim to challenge this by investigating how radial geometry, current density, and magnetic field strength control the coupled evolution of rotation and heating that dictates λ.
AI.method: A reduced two-temperature magnetohydrodynamic model is developed to determine how radial geometry, current density, and magnetic field strength control rotation and heating. The model is benchmarked against Ar and Ar/Kr experiments spanning current densities up to 15 kA/m^2, magnetic fields up to 0.57 T, feed pressures of 0.5-3 Torr, and annulus sizes of 1-5 cm. The model is then applied to 40Ar/36Ar isotopic mixture simulations.
AI.result: Volumetric Lorentz forcing sustains higher λ and greater local compositional shifts throughout a larger radial portion of the fluid than wall-bounded shear centrifuges, despite lower peak λ. Joint optimization of electromagnetic force and geometry enables EMDCs to exceed the separative performance of shear-driven centrifuges operating near material speed limits, even with lower area-averaged λ.
AI.conclusion: The results challenge the assertion that viscous dissipation constrains weakly ionized plasma centrifuges to λ<1, and indicate that enhanced radial mass separation is best achieved by increasing the radial distribution of λ rather than maximizing its peak or area-averaged value.

title: Incompressible Navier-Stokes-Fourier limit from a nonlinear quantum Fokker-Planck equation
summary: We derive the incompressible Navier-Stokes-Fourier limit from a nonlinear quantum Fokker-Planck equation with Bose-Einstein or Fermi-Dirac statistics. The model has a self-consistent collision structure, with the local density acting as the collision frequency and the bulk velocity and temperature determined by nonlinear quantum-weighted moments of the distribution. We work near a global quantum equilibrium under the diffusive scaling and keep the quantum parameter fixed. Uniform estimates with respect to the Knudsen number yield strong microscopic relaxation and identify the limiting infinitesimal quantum equilibrium. Using the local conservation laws, we prove the incompressibility condition, the Boussinesq relation, and strong compactness of the divergence-free velocity component and a quantum-adapted thermal mode, while the acoustic modes vanish locally by a dispersive estimate. The limiting viscous stress tensor and heat flux are identified by solving auxiliary equations for the linearized quantum Fokker-Planck operator and by expanding the local quantum equilibrium manifold. The resulting incompressible Navier-Stokes-Fourier system retains the effect of quantum statistics through its normalization constants and transport coefficients.

AI.tldr: The paper derives the incompressible Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations as a hydrodynamic limit from a nonlinear quantum Fokker-Planck equation with Bose-Einstein or Fermi-Dirac statistics under diffusive scaling, preserving quantum effects in transport coefficients.
AI.motivation: To rigorously establish the hydrodynamic limit of quantum kinetic equations, showing how quantum statistics (Bose-Einstein/Fermi-Dirac) influence macroscopic fluid behavior while keeping the quantum parameter fixed.
AI.method: The authors work under diffusive scaling near a global quantum equilibrium with fixed quantum parameter. They use uniform estimates with respect to the Knudsen number to obtain strong microscopic relaxation, identify the limiting infinitesimal quantum equilibrium, and exploit local conservation laws to prove incompressibility, the Boussinesq relation, and strong compactness. Dispersive estimates eliminate acoustic modes, and the viscous/heat transport coefficients are derived by solving auxiliary linearized equations and expanding the local quantum equilibrium manifold.
AI.result: The limiting system is the incompressible Navier-Stokes-Fourier system, which retains quantum statistics through its normalization constants and transport coefficients. Strong convergence of the divergence-free velocity component and a quantum-adapted thermal mode is established.
AI.conclusion: Quantum statistics survive in the hydrodynamic regime, modifying the macroscopic fluid equations in a rigorous and quantitative way, with explicit contributions appearing in transport coefficients and normalization constants.

title: Design principles for energy dissipation in viscoelastic network metamaterials
summary: Mechanical energy dissipation in networked materials is relevant for applications from vibration isolation to impact protection, yet identifying optimal dissipative architectures in large disordered truss networks is computationally prohibitive with conventional finite element methods. We develop an efficient graph Laplacian-based spectral framework for viscoelastic truss networks, in which the full continuum dynamics of each rod are retained exactly and the problem size scales with the number of joints rather than element-level discretization points. Using this framework, we investigate how redistributing cross-sectional areas within a network (without changing material composition) controls energy dissipation. We find that random redistribution typically reduces dissipation relative to a uniform baseline, while gradient-based optimization yields nontrivial architectures whose form is governed by the intrinsic attenuation length of the base material. Focusing on driving frequencies near a global resonant mode of the network, we show that the optimal mass distribution decays from the source (driven joint) with the attenuation length scale, and at small attenuation lengths the optimal architecture is independent of the boundary conditions. These results motivate future studies of dissipation length scale based design principles on more complex disordered architectures and provide an efficient computational framework for exploring such structures at scale.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an efficient graph Laplacian-based spectral framework for viscoelastic truss networks that retains exact continuum rod dynamics while scaling with the number of joints rather than discretization points. Using this framework, the authors study how redistributing cross-sectional areas controls energy dissipation, finding that random redistribution typically reduces dissipation, while gradient-based optimization yields architectures whose form is governed by the intrinsic attenuation length of the base material.
AI.motivation: Identifying optimal dissipative architectures in large disordered truss networks is computationally prohibitive with conventional finite element methods, yet mechanical energy dissipation in networked materials is relevant for applications from vibration isolation to impact protection.
AI.method: Develops an efficient graph Laplacian-based spectral framework for viscoelastic truss networks that retains full continuum dynamics of each rod exactly while scaling problem size with the number of joints rather than element-level discretization points. The framework is used to investigate how redistributing cross-sectional areas controls energy dissipation, comparing random redistribution and gradient-based optimization approaches.
AI.result: Random redistribution typically reduces dissipation relative to a uniform baseline, while gradient-based optimization yields nontrivial architectures governed by the intrinsic attenuation length. Near a global resonant mode, the optimal mass distribution decays from the driven joint with the attenuation length scale, and at small attenuation lengths the optimal architecture becomes independent of boundary conditions.
AI.conclusion: The results motivate future studies of dissipation-length-scale-based design principles for more complex disordered architectures and provide an efficient computational framework for exploring such structures at scale.

title: A spectral-compensated scheme for space-parameter Poisson noise functionals: error bounds and complexity estimates
summary: This paper computes Poisson space noise functionals, $P^{\prime}(u)$, realised in a Gel'fand triple built from a Lévy measure $λ_β(u)du$. We isolate three discretisation parameters: a small-amplitude cut-off, a Donsker delta truncation M, and a chaos order N. For a stable-type intensity $λ_β(u)=cu^{-1-α}$ ($0<α<2$), replacing discarded small amplitudes with matched Gaussian space noise improves the Wasserstein-1 error from $O(ε^{1-α/2})$ to $O(ε)$. The residual is asymptotically normal at $O(ε^{α/2})$. This compensation reduces computational complexity from $O(τ^{-2α/(2-α)})$ to $O(τ^{-α})$. We also evaluate the Gamma-type boundary ($α=0$) and exponential tempering. Truncations converge algebraically (M) and super-geometrically (N). All predicted rates are tightly confirmed by deterministic numerical experiments via Gil-Pelaez inversion, eliminating Monte Carlo noise.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes Poisson space noise functionals by splitting discretization into three parameters (amplitude cut-off, Donsker delta truncation, chaos order). For stable-type intensities, replacing discarded small amplitudes with matched Gaussian noise improves Wasserstein-1 error from O(ε^{1-α/2}) to O(ε), with asymptotically normal residuals, reducing computational complexity from O(τ^{-2α/(2-α)}) to O(τ^{-α}). All rates verified via Gil-Pelaez inversion without Monte Carlo noise.
AI.motivation: To improve the accuracy and computational efficiency of approximating Poisson space noise functionals by understanding and compensating for the errors introduced when truncating small-amplitude jumps in Lévy-driven noise processes.
AI.method: The paper constructs a Gel'fand triple from a Lévy measure and isolates three discretization parameters (amplitude cut-off ε, Donsker delta truncation M, chaos order N). For stable-type intensities, discarded small amplitudes are replaced with matched Gaussian space noise. Error rates are derived and verified through deterministic numerical experiments using Gil-Pelaez inversion.
AI.result: Wasserstein-1 error improves from O(ε^{1-α/2}) to O(ε) via Gaussian compensation for stable-type intensities (0<α<2). Residual is asymptotically normal at O(ε^{α/2}). Computational complexity reduces from O(τ^{-2α/(2-α)}) to O(τ^{-α}). Gamma-type boundary (α=0) and exponential tempering are also analyzed. Truncations converge algebraically (M) and super-geometrically (N). All predicted rates are tightly confirmed numerically.
AI.conclusion: Gaussian compensation of discarded small amplitudes significantly improves both error rates and computational complexity for Poisson space noise approximations. The derived asymptotic rates are precisely validated by deterministic numerical experiments, providing a rigorous framework for efficient noise simulation.

title: Variational Formulation of a Hybrid Kinetic and Gyrokinetic Model for Astrophysical and Laboratory Plasmas
summary: We present a Lagrangian model that encapsulates fully kinetic ions and gyrokinetic electrons for solar wind electromagnetic turbulence. Using a consistent method, where both electrons and protons are treated with the same mathematical formalism, we derive and implement a model in which high-frequency waves and kinetic electron effects are described in a computationally cost-efficient way. Higher-order Lie-transform perturbation methods applied to Hamiltonian formulation of guiding center motion are used to describe the dynamics of particles and fields. We use a variational approach to derive field equations for closure of the system.

AI.tldr: A Lagrangian-based hybrid model combining fully kinetic ions with gyrokinetic electrons is developed for solar wind electromagnetic turbulence, using a unified mathematical formalism for both species and Lie-transform perturbation methods for computational efficiency.
AI.motivation: Solar wind electromagnetic turbulence involves both kinetic ion and electron effects, but fully kinetic treatments of both species are computationally prohibitive. A consistent hybrid approach is needed to capture high-frequency waves and kinetic electron physics efficiently.
AI.method: The model treats ions as fully kinetic and electrons as gyrokinetic, using the same Hamiltonian guiding-center formalism for both. Higher-order Lie-transform perturbation theory describes particle and field dynamics, and a variational approach derives field equations for closure.
AI.result: The paper presents a computationally cost-efficient model that captures high-frequency waves and kinetic electron effects while maintaining consistency between electron and proton treatments through a unified mathematical framework.
AI.conclusion: A self-consistent, computationally efficient kinetic-gyrokinetic hybrid model for solar wind turbulence is established using Hamiltonian and variational principles, enabling simulation of electromagnetic turbulence with kinetic ion and electron physics.

title: On The Minkowski Problem With Respect To A Mixed Euclidean-Gaussian Density
summary: In this paper, we pose a new class of Minkowski problems corresponding to the mixed Euclidean-Gaussian volume. Using the flow method, we prove the existence of smooth normalized solutions for the corresponding Monge-Ampère-type equation in the symmetric case. Then, by approximation, we obtain the existence of origin-symmetric solutions to the mixed Euclidean-Gaussian Minkowski problem.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new class of Minkowski problems related to mixed Euclidean-Gaussian volume. Using a flow method, the authors prove the existence of smooth normalized solutions for the associated Monge-Ampère-type equation in the symmetric case, and then via approximation obtain origin-symmetric solutions to the mixed Euclidean-Gaussian Minkowski problem.
AI.motivation: To extend the classical Minkowski problem to a new setting involving mixed Euclidean-Gaussian volume, thereby constructing a novel class of geometric variational problems and establishing existence of solutions.
AI.method: The authors employ a flow method to establish the existence of smooth normalized solutions to the corresponding Monge-Ampère-type equation in the symmetric case, followed by an approximation argument to obtain origin-symmetric solutions to the mixed Euclidean-Gaussian Minkowski problem.
AI.result: Existence of smooth normalized solutions for the Monge-Ampère-type equation in the symmetric case, and existence of origin-symmetric solutions to the mixed Euclidean-Gaussian Minkowski problem via approximation.
AI.conclusion: The mixed Euclidean-Gaussian Minkowski problem is solvable in the origin-symmetric setting, generalizing previous Minkowski problem results to this mixed volume framework.

title: Nonlinear Fourier spectral signatures of rogue waves observed in Bose-Einstein condensates
summary: Modulation instability provides an important framework for understanding rogue wave (RW) formation on continuous backgrounds. However, the formation mechanism and nonlinear spectral structures of RWs in Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) matter-wave systems with vanishing boundary conditions remain largely unexplored. Here, we employ the nonlinear Fourier transform (NFT), based on the integrable structure of the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation and the Zakharov-Shabat scattering problem, to investigate two representative classes of first-order RWs in BEC systems. Through nonlinear spectral analysis and Darboux reconstruction, we demonstrate that both Gaussian-wave-packet-induced extreme localization events and experimentally observed Peregrine solitons are governed by the coherent dynamics of discrete soliton modes encoded in the nonlinear spectrum. For Gaussian initial states, increasing the initial width leads to an increasing number of discrete eigenvalues, resulting in a transition from fundamental solitons and bound states to Christmas-tree-like RW structures. For experimentally observed Peregrine solitons, localized perturbations reshape the discrete spectral configuration and phase evolution, enabling coherent focusing of multiple bound soliton modes. Furthermore, we reveal the spectral mechanism of higher-order RWs and propose an inverse spectral-engineering approach based on discrete-spectrum phase matching. Our results provide a nonlinear spectral perspective for understanding and controlling RW formation in matter-wave systems with vanishing boundary conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper uses nonlinear Fourier transform (NFT) analysis to investigate rogue wave (RW) formation in Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) systems with vanishing boundary conditions, revealing that both Gaussian-wave-packet-induced extreme localization and Peregrine solitons are governed by coherent dynamics of discrete soliton modes. The authors uncover spectral mechanisms of higher-order RWs and propose inverse spectral engineering via discrete-spectrum phase matching.
AI.motivation: While modulation instability is a well-established framework for understanding rogue wave formation on continuous backgrounds, the formation mechanisms and nonlinear spectral structures of RWs in BEC matter-wave systems with vanishing boundary conditions remain largely unexplored, creating a gap in understanding RW physics in this important regime.
AI.method: The authors employ the nonlinear Fourier transform (NFT), based on the integrable structure of the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation and the Zakharov-Shabat scattering problem, combined with Darboux reconstruction to analyze two representative classes of first-order RWs in BEC systems.
AI.result: For Gaussian initial states, increasing initial width increases the number of discrete eigenvalues, causing a transition from fundamental solitons and bound states to Christmas-tree-like RW structures.
