title: Signatures of kinetic gravity braiding in cosmological probes of the gravitational field
summary: We study the observational signatures of kinetic gravity braiding (KGB) models in relativistic cosmological probes constructed along the past light cone. Using the relativistic $N$-body code KGB-evolution, we generate light-cone outputs and compute several observables that directly probe the gravitational field, including weak gravitational lensing convergence, Shapiro time delay, the integrated Sachs-Wolfe and Rees-Sciama (ISW-RS) effects, and gravitational redshift. Full-sky maps and angular power spectra of these quantities are constructed and compared with $k$-essence models and predictions from linear perturbation theory. We find that the derivative coupling between the scalar field and the metric modifies both the amplitude and the time evolution of the gravitational potentials, producing scale-dependent deviations ranging from a few percent to tens of percent. In particular, the ISW-RS signal exhibits the largest fractional response, as the slower decay of the Weyl potential suppresses the KGB signal in the ISW-dominated regime, whereas nonlinear evolution reverses this trend at higher multipoles, producing differences of tens of percent relative to $k$-essence. Weak gravitational lensing also provides a strong complementary probe and, for the model considered here, exhibits clear deviations from the $k$-essence prediction at small scales with enhancements up to $\sim 10$-$12\%$ at multipoles $\ell \sim 10^2$-$10^3$. Our results show that linear perturbation theory accurately describes the large-scale behaviour, while nonlinear effects become important at smaller scales, particularly for the ISW-RS signal and, more moderately, for the convergence, and must therefore be included for reliable theoretical predictions.

AI.tldr: This paper studies observational signatures of kinetic gravity braiding (KGB) models using relativistic N-body simulations, computing light-cone observables like weak lensing, Shapiro time delay, ISW-RS effects, and gravitational redshift. They find scale-dependent deviations from k-essence models, with the ISW-RS signal showing the largest fractional response (tens of percent) and weak lensing showing up to 10-12% enhancements at small scales, while linear theory works at large scales but nonlinear effects matter at small scales.
AI.motivation: To understand how kinetic gravity braiding (KGB) models, which feature derivative coupling between scalar field and metric, manifest in relativistic cosmological observables along the past light cone, and to determine where linear perturbation theory breaks down in favor of nonlinear effects.
AI.method: Using the relativistic N-body code KGB-evolution to generate light-cone outputs, constructing full-sky maps and angular power spectra of gravitational observables (weak lensing convergence, Shapiro time delay, ISW-RS effects, gravitational redshift), and comparing with k-essence models and linear perturbation theory predictions.
AI.result: The derivative coupling modifies gravitational potential amplitudes and time evolution, producing scale-dependent deviations from a few to tens of percent. ISW-RS shows the largest fractional response due to slower Weyl potential decay, with nonlinear effects reversing trends at higher multipoles. Weak lensing shows clear deviations from k-essence with 10-12% enhancements at multipoles 10^2-10^3. Linear theory works at large scales but fails at small scales, especially for ISW-RS.
AI.conclusion: KGB models produce distinctive observational signatures in relativistic probes, particularly in ISW-RS and weak lensing, and nonlinear effects must be included for reliable theoretical predictions at small scales, as linear perturbation theory alone is insufficient.

title: A MATLAB Tool for the Stable Generation of Matrix Polynomial Evaluation Schemes with Two-Product Savings
summary: Computing numerical approximations of matrix functions frequently relies on the efficient evaluation of high-degree matrix polynomials. Although computational bounds are historically governed by the Paterson--Stockmeyer (PS) method, recent theoretical developments have demonstrated the viability of evaluation schemes that eliminate two matrix products ($2M$). Existing literature documents stable instances of this $2M$ reduction only for isolated cases, such as specific degrees of Taylor approximations for the matrix exponential and the matrix logarithm. However, a generalized approach for arbitrary polynomials remains unestablished. To address this limitation, this work presents a software-driven procedure that extends these computational savings to polynomials of degrees $m \in \{18, 21, 24, 26, 27, 28\}$ and all $m \ge 30$, requiring primarily a non-zero leading coefficient. Since the underlying evaluation coefficients must be determined by solving systems of nonlinear equations (SNEs), selecting a numerically stable solution set is critical. We introduce an automated verification routine designed to filter and validate robust coefficient sets for floating-point execution. The primary contribution is a MATLAB implementation leveraging variable precision arithmetic to handle the underlying SNEs, verify stability, and project precision bounds. Numerical experiments involving various matrix functions verify that the developed implementation preserves or, in some instances, enhances the numerical accuracy of the classic PS method, while systematically achieving the theoretical reduction of $2M$.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a software-driven approach to achieve a 2-matrix-product reduction in matrix polynomial evaluation for arbitrary degrees (m ∈ {18, 21, 24, 26, 27, 28} and all m ≥ 30), extending beyond isolated cases previously documented. The method uses variable precision arithmetic in MATLAB to solve systems of nonlinear equations for evaluation coefficients, with an automated verification routine ensuring numerical stability.
AI.motivation: The Paterson-Stockmeyer (PS) method has historically governed computational bounds for evaluating high-degree matrix polynomials. While theoretical work has shown that certain evaluation schemes can eliminate two matrix products (2M reduction), this has only been demonstrated for isolated cases (specific Taylor degree approximations for matrix exponential and logarithm). A generalized approach for arbitrary polynomials remains unestablished, limiting the practical impact of this theoretical improvement.
AI.method: The paper develops a generalized procedure that extends 2M computational savings to polynomials of degrees m ∈ {18, 21, 24, 26, 27, 28} and all m ≥ 30, requiring primarily a non-zero leading coefficient. The approach involves: (1) solving systems of nonlinear equations (SNEs) to determine evaluation coefficients, (2) an automated verification routine to filter and validate numerically stable coefficient sets for floating-point execution, and (3) a MATLAB implementation using variable precision arithmetic to handle SNEs, verify stability, and project precision bounds.
AI.result: Numerical experiments across various matrix functions verify that the implementation preserves or, in some instances, enhances the numerical accuracy of the classic PS method while systematically achieving the theoretical 2M reduction.
AI.conclusion: The work successfully establishes a generalized, software-driven framework for achieving 2M computational savings in matrix polynomial evaluation, extending the previously isolated results to a broad range of polynomial degrees, with numerical stability validated through automated verification in a variable precision arithmetic MATLAB implementation.

title: Isolated Singularities and Measure Data Problems for Semilinear Equations Driven by Stable Lévy Operators
summary: We investigate positive solutions of semilinear equations driven by uniformly elliptic strictly $2s$-stable Lévy operators, where $s\in (0,1)$. We first prove that every positive distributional solution of $-Lu=u^p$ in a punctured domain $D\setminus\{0\}$ satisfies $-Lu=u^p+kδ_0$ in $D$ for some $k\ge0$, and that necessarily $k=0$ whenever $p\ge d/(d-2s)$. We then study the corresponding Dirichlet problem in which the Dirac mass is replaced by a bounded positive measure, and establish the existence of a critical parameter $k_μ$: below this threshold minimal positive solutions exist, whereas above it the problem admits no solution. In the symmetric case, we further prove multiplicity below the threshold, as well as existence and uniqueness at the threshold itself.

AI.tldr: This paper studies positive solutions of semilinear equations driven by uniformly elliptic strictly 2s-stable Lévy operators, proving removability of isolated singularities, existence of critical threshold parameters for Dirac mass problems, and multiplicity results in the symmetric case.
AI.motivation: To understand the behavior of positive solutions to semilinear elliptic equations with stable Lévy operators near isolated singularities (punctured domains) and to characterize when singular sources can or cannot exist, extending classical results for fractional Laplacians to more general stable Lévy operators.
AI.method: The authors analyze positive distributional solutions on punctured domains, proving they can be extended with possible Dirac mass at the singularity. They establish conditions under which the Dirac mass must vanish, then study Dirichlet problems with bounded positive measures, identifying a critical parameter threshold via comparison/barrier methods and symmetry-based arguments.
AI.result: (1) Every positive distributional solution on a punctured domain satisfies -Lu = u^p + kδ_0 for some k≥0, with k=0 necessarily when p≥d/(d-2s). (2) For the Dirichlet problem with bounded positive measures, a critical parameter k_μ exists: minimal positive solutions exist below it, none above it. (3) In the symmetric case, multiplicity below the threshold and existence/uniqueness at the threshold are proven.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a complete characterization of isolated singularities and critical thresholds for semilinear problems driven by general strictly 2s-stable Lévy operators, extending prior results from the fractional Laplacian case to broader nonlocal operator classes, including multiplicity phenomena in the symmetric setting.

title: Large-Time-Step Operation in a Volume Integral Equation for Dielectric Scattering
summary: In transient electromagnetic analysis, explicit time-domain solvers are restricted by the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) condition, making finely discretized dielectric scattering problems computationally expensive. This work investigates large-time-step operation in a marching-on-in-time time-domain current-density volume integral equation (MOT-JVIE) solver for dielectric scattering. For the considered band-limited excitations, accurate transient analysis is demonstrated for time steps up to 16 times larger than the reference CFL-limited time step associated with the voxel discretization. The study reveals a fundamental computational shift in the large-time-step regime. As the time-step size increases, the present-time causal interaction region expands, increasing the number of nonzero entries in the present-time interaction matrix and causing the dominant computational cost to transition from history-term evaluations to repeated matrix--vector products involving this matrix. Consequently, the present-time interaction matrix emerges as the principal scalability bottleneck in the large-time-step regime. To address this bottleneck, a matrix-free FFT-based matrix--vector-product strategy that exploits the multilevel Toeplitz structure of the Green-function-related volume-integral operator is employed for the present-time interaction matrix. The proposed framework is evaluated through an inhomogeneous dielectric cube and an 8 X 8 array of inhomogeneous dielectric nanopillars representative of multiscale metasurface structures, demonstrating more than an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost. In single-threaded execution, the method is demonstrated for 15.6 million unknowns, providing a large-scale MOT-JVIE demonstration beyond 15 million unknowns on one CPU thread.

AI.tldr: This paper explores large-time-step operation in a marching-on-in-time time-domain current-density volume integral equation (MOT-JVIE) solver for dielectric scattering, demonstrating accurate transient analysis with time steps up to 16x larger than the CFL limit. It identifies the present-time interaction matrix as the main scalability bottleneck in this regime and employs a matrix-free FFT-based approach exploiting the multilevel Toeplitz structure to achieve over an order-of-magnitude computational cost reduction, demonstrated on 15.6 million unknowns.
AI.motivation: Explicit time-domain solvers are limited by the CFL condition, making finely discretized dielectric scattering problems computationally prohibitive. The authors seek to overcome this restriction by enabling large-time-step operation in MOT-JVIE solvers while addressing the resulting computational challenges.
AI.method: The paper investigates the computational behavior of MOT-JVIE in the large-time-step regime, showing that as time steps grow, the present-time causal interaction region expands and the present-time interaction matrix becomes the dominant cost. To mitigate this, a matrix-free FFT-based matrix-vector-product strategy exploiting the multilevel Toeplitz structure of the Green-function-related volume-integral operator is applied to the present-time interaction matrix.
AI.result: Accurate transient analysis is demonstrated for time steps up to 16x larger than the CFL-limited step. On inhomogeneous dielectric cube and 8x8 nanopillar array examples, more than an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost is achieved. Single-threaded execution is demonstrated for 15.6 million unknowns, marking the first MOT-JVIE demonstration beyond 15 million unknowns on one CPU thread.
AI.conclusion: The proposed matrix-free FFT-based framework effectively addresses the scalability bottleneck of the present-time interaction matrix in large-time-step MOT-JVIE, enabling substantial computational savings and supporting very large-scale dielectric scattering simulations on a single CPU thread.

title: Galerkin method for asymmetrically-weighted Hermite approximations applied to the Vlasov-Poisson system
summary: We investigate a numerical method for the Vlasov-Poisson (VP) system utilizing asymmetrically-weighted (AW) Hermite bases in velocity space, which is an hyperbolic system. In particular, we concentrate on spectral methods in velocity. For the Hermite spectral form of the VP system, we analyze the resaon that the form with AW Hermite bases can be instable. To obtain L2 stability properties, we consider a Galerkin method intead of the classical Petrov-Galerkin method, which naturally ensures stability with respect to the L2 norm. We also present an equivalent form of the method that maintains a computational cost modest compared to that of the Petrov-Galerkin method. Finally, we present numerical simulations based on the proposed Hermite spectral method, showcasing its stability.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates a numerical method for the Vlasov-Poisson (VP) system using asymmetrically-weighted (AW) Hermite bases in velocity space. The authors identify why the AW Hermite spectral form can be unstable, and propose a Galerkin method (instead of the classical Petrov-Galerkin method) that ensures L2 stability. They present an equivalent computationally efficient formulation and validate the method's stability through numerical simulations.
AI.motivation: The VP system is a hyperbolic system, and while Hermite spectral methods are attractive for velocity-space discretization, the asymmetrically-weighted Hermite basis formulation can suffer from instabilities. Understanding and overcoming this instability is essential for reliable numerical simulation.
AI.method: The authors analyze the instability of the AW Hermite spectral form of the VP system. They propose switching from the classical Petrov-Galerkin method to a Galerkin method, which naturally provides L2 norm stability. They further develop an equivalent formulation that keeps computational costs comparable to the Petrov-Galerkin approach.
AI.result: The proposed Galerkin-based Hermite spectral method demonstrates stable numerical behavior in simulations of the Vlasov-Poisson system, while maintaining modest computational cost.
AI.conclusion: A stable and computationally efficient Hermite spectral method for the VP system is achieved by adopting a Galerkin framework with asymmetric Hermite bases, resolving the inherent instability of the traditional Petrov-Galerkin formulation.

title: A parametrix construction for time-fractional partial differential equations
comment: 18 pages. Materials originally included in the first version of arXiv:2511.04885
summary: We prove in detail how to construct the parametrix of a parameter-dependent family of pseudodifferential operators, appearing in the analysis of time-fractional partial differential equations. In particular, we perform a precise study of the dependence from the parameter of the corresponding asymptotic expansion terms, as well as of the smoothing remainders. Moreover, we provide some results about the Laplace transform of vector-valued distributions, also appearing in the analysis of time-fractional partial differential equations.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a detailed construction of the parametrix (approximate inverse) for parameter-dependent families of pseudodifferential operators relevant to time-fractional PDEs, including a precise analysis of the parameter dependence in asymptotic expansion terms and smoothing remainders, along with results on Laplace transforms of vector-valued distributions.
AI.motivation: Time-fractional partial differential equations require sophisticated analytic tools. Understanding the parametrix of parameter-dependent pseudodifferential operators is essential for analyzing solutions of such equations, as the parameter typically relates to time-fractional order or Laplace transform variables.
AI.method: The authors provide a rigorous, detailed construction of the parametrix for parameter-dependent families of pseudodifferential operators. They carefully track the dependence of the asymptotic expansion terms and smoothing remainders on the parameter. They also develop results concerning the Laplace transform of vector-valued distributions, which are also relevant to time-fractional PDE analysis.
AI.result: A complete and detailed proof of the parametrix construction for parameter-dependent pseudodifferential operators is presented, with precise control over the parameter dependence in both the asymptotic expansions and the smoothing remainder terms. Additionally, new results on Laplace transforms of vector-valued distributions are provided.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes the necessary analytical foundations—parametrix construction with precise parameter tracking and Laplace transform results for vector-valued distributions—that are crucial for the analysis of time-fractional partial differential equations.

title: Graph Neural Network Force Fields for Spin Dynamics in Metallic Magnets
summary: Metallic magnets exhibit complex spin dynamics governed by electronically generated interactions. Predictive simulations of such dynamics typically require repeated solutions of an underlying electronic problem throughout the time evolution, creating a major computational bottleneck. Here we introduce a graph neural network (GNN) magnetic force-field framework that learns the effective magnetic energy functional governing itinerant spin dynamics directly from electronic calculations. Conceptually analogous to machine-learned interatomic potentials, the proposed framework enables efficient evaluation of spin torques while capturing the nonlinear and spatially extended interactions generated by itinerant electrons. We benchmark the method on representative metallic magnetic systems exhibiting collinear, noncollinear, and noncoplanar magnetic order. The learned force fields accurately reproduce electronically generated spin torques and yield nonequilibrium spin dynamics in excellent agreement with direct electronic simulations. Our results establish graph neural networks as a powerful framework for machine-learned magnetic force fields, providing a pathway toward predictive large-scale simulations of nonequilibrium magnetism across multiple length and time scales.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a graph neural network (GNN)-based magnetic force-field framework that learns the effective magnetic energy functional for itinerant spin dynamics directly from electronic structure calculations, enabling efficient spin torque evaluation and large-scale predictive simulations of nonequilibrium magnetism.
AI.motivation: Predictive simulations of metallic magnet spin dynamics require repeatedly solving the underlying electronic problem during time evolution, creating a major computational bottleneck that limits simulation scale and accessibility.
AI.method: The authors develop a GNN magnetic force-field framework that learns the effective magnetic energy functional from electronic calculations, analogous to machine-learned interatomic potentials. This enables efficient spin torque evaluation while capturing nonlinear and spatially extended interactions from itinerant electrons.
AI.result: The GNN force fields accurately reproduce electronically generated spin torques and yield nonequilibrium spin dynamics in excellent agreement with direct electronic simulations across collinear, noncollinear, and noncoplanar magnetic order benchmark systems.
AI.conclusion: Graph neural networks are established as a powerful framework for machine-learned magnetic force fields, providing a pathway toward predictive large-scale simulations of nonequilibrium magnetism across multiple length and time scales.

title: Windowed thinning and query complexity for the bouncy particle and Zigzag samplers
summary: Let $μ(d x)\propto e^{-U(x)} d x$ on $\R^d$, where $U$ is $m$-strongly convex and $L$-smooth, and denote by $κ=L/m$ the condition number. We consider windowed thinning, an exact simulation method for the bouncy particle sampler and the coordinate Zigzag process. The method divides a trajectory into deterministic windows and uses a gradient evaluation at the beginning of each window to construct a tractable local envelope for the event rate. Combining this construction with quantitative mixing estimates and finite-time bounds on the expected numbers of bounces and flips yields query complexity guarantees from a Gaussian cold start. For total-variation error $\varepsilon$, the expected query counts are $O(κ^{1/2}d\,(d\logκ+\log\frac1\varepsilon))$ gradient queries for the bouncy particle sampler and $O(κd^{1/4}(d\logκ+\log\frac1\varepsilon))$ full-gradient equivalents for Zigzag, where $d$ coordinate-partial queries count as one equivalent.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the query complexity of windowed thinning, an exact simulation method for the bouncy particle sampler (BPS) and coordinate Zigzag process, providing explicit gradient query complexity guarantees from a Gaussian cold start under strong convexity and smoothness assumptions.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to provide quantitative complexity guarantees for exact piecewise-deterministic Markov process (PDMP) samplers like BPS and Zigzag, which previously lacked clear finite-time query complexity bounds despite their practical success.
AI.method: The method combines windowed thinning (dividing trajectories into deterministic windows with a local envelope for the event rate built from a gradient evaluation at each window start) with quantitative mixing estimates and finite-time bounds on expected bounce/flip counts to derive total query complexity from a Gaussian cold start.
AI.result: For total-variation error epsilon: BPS requires O(kappa^{1/2} d (d log kappa + log 1/epsilon)) gradient queries, and Zigzag requires O(kappa d^{1/4} (d log kappa + log 1/epsilon)) full-gradient equivalents (where d coordinate-partial queries count as one equivalent).
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes the first explicit gradient query complexity guarantees for windowed thinning applied to BPS and Zigzag under log-concave targets, showing polynomial dependence on dimension d and condition number kappa with the mixing complexity scaling favorably in kappa.

title: Osgood meets Ambrosio-DiPerna-Lions
summary: In this note we extend the Ambrosio-DiPerna-Lions theory on the well-posedness of the transport equation to the case in which the vector field satisfies an $L^p$ Osgood condition. In particular we show that bounded distributional solutions to the transport equation are unique and thus renormalized. As opposed to the classical proof, we do not rely on the vanishing of a commutator, but we show that a weighted energy built out of the Littlewood-Paley decomposition of the solution is conserved.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the Ambrosio-DiPerna-Lions theory for well-posedness of transport equations to vector fields satisfying an L^p Osgood condition, proving uniqueness and renormalization of bounded distributional solutions via a new weighted energy approach based on Littlewood-Paley decomposition, avoiding the classical commutator argument.
AI.motivation: The classical Ambrosio-DiPerna-Lions theory establishes well-posedness of the transport equation under Sobolev regularity assumptions on the vector field. This paper aims to broaden the applicability of this theory by relaxing the regularity condition to an L^p Osgood condition, which is a more general and flexible criterion.
AI.method: Instead of relying on the vanishing of a commutator (as in the classical proof), the authors demonstrate that a weighted energy constructed from the Littlewood-Paley decomposition of the solution is conserved. This weighted energy approach provides the key mechanism to prove uniqueness of bounded distributional solutions.
AI.result: The authors show that bounded distributional solutions to the transport equation are unique and therefore renormalized under the L^p Osgood condition on the vector field.
AI.conclusion: The Ambrosio-DiPerna-Lions well-posedness theory is successfully extended to vector fields satisfying an L^p Osgood condition, achieved through a novel weighted energy conservation argument based on Littlewood-Paley decomposition rather than the traditional commutator method.

title: Frequency-Domain Analysis of Wave Scattering by Spatially Dispersive Metasurfaces Using the Method of Auxiliary Sources
summary: Spatially dispersive metasurfaces exhibit angle-dependent responses that cannot be accurately modeled using conventional local susceptibilities. Extended Generalized Sheet Transition Conditions (GSTCs) have been introduced to account for spatial dispersion by incorporating spatial derivatives of the electromagnetic fields. In this work, these extended GSTCs are integrated into the Method of Auxiliary Sources (MAS), resulting in a meshless simulation framework for the analysis of spatially dispersive metasurfaces. The proposed formulation is developed for infinite planar, finite planar, polygon shaped, and cylindrical metasurfaces, while it is general and also applicable to bianisotropic spatially dispersive metasurfaces. For validation, the numerical examples consider Lorentz-type spatial resonators, consistent with previously published studies. The extended GSTCs are enforced within the MAS via appropriate placement of auxiliary sources. Numerical results are presented for several geometries, including planar, polygonal, semicircular, and cylindrical metasurfaces. The obtained results show very good agreement with previously published data, demonstrating the accuracy and flexibility of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: This work integrates Extended Generalized Sheet Transition Conditions (GSTCs), which account for spatial dispersion in metasurfaces, into the Method of Auxiliary Sources (MAS), creating a meshless simulation framework. The method handles infinite planar, finite planar, polygon, and cylindrical geometries and is validated against published results with good agreement.
AI.motivation: Conventional local susceptibilities cannot accurately model spatially dispersive metasurfaces that exhibit angle-dependent responses, necessitating extended GSTCs that incorporate spatial derivatives of electromagnetic fields. A versatile numerical framework to simulate such metasurfaces across various geometries is needed.
AI.method: Extended GSTCs (accounting for spatial dispersion) are integrated into the Method of Auxiliary Sources (MAS). Extended GSTCs are enforced via appropriate placement of auxiliary sources. The formulation is developed for infinite planar, finite planar, polygon-shaped, and cylindrical metasurfaces, and is general enough to handle bianisotropic spatially dispersive metasurfaces.
AI.result: Numerical results are presented for planar, polygonal, semicircular, and cylindrical metasurface geometries using Lorentz-type spatial resonators. The results show very good agreement with previously published data, demonstrating accuracy and flexibility of the proposed method.
AI.conclusion: The proposed meshless framework based on extended GSTCs integrated into MAS is accurate and flexible for analyzing spatially dispersive metasurfaces across multiple geometries, validated against existing published results.

title: Graph Neural Multilevel Preconditioners for Iterative Solvers
summary: Solving large, sparse linear systems is a core task in scientific computing, and efficient iterative solvers rely critically on effective and robust preconditioning. While classical methods such as algebraic multigrid (AMG) are highly scalable, their robustness can degrade on indefinite or nonsymmetric systems where heuristics originally developed for elliptic PDEs are less reliable. Recently, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as data-driven preconditioners; yet, the practical impact of imposing an AMG-style hierarchy remains underexplored for general sparse matrices. In this work, we propose a Graph Neural Multilevel Preconditioner (GMP) that adopts an AMG hierarchy as a structural prior and learns smoothing, restriction, and interpolation operators in a unified framework. Our method targets general sparse systems and is instantiated as a drop-in preconditioner for standard Krylov solvers. On a benchmark of over 800 sparse matrices, we compare against classical AMG, single-level ILUT, and state-of-the-art GNN preconditioners, and characterize the regimes where multilevel graph neural preconditioning improves convergence or, conversely, introduces overhead relative to strong single-level baselines. These results highlight both the promise and the limitations of enforcing AMG-style multilevel structure in learned preconditioners for large-scale scientific simulations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Graph Neural Multilevel Preconditioner (GMP) that incorporates an AMG hierarchy as a structural prior, learning smoothing, restriction, and interpolation operators in a unified GNN framework for general sparse linear systems. Tested on 800+ matrices, it compares against classical AMG, ILUT, and GNN preconditioners, showing both improvements and limitations of enforcing multilevel structure.
AI.motivation: Classical AMG preconditioners are scalable but their robustness degrades on indefinite or nonsymmetric systems. GNN-based preconditioners exist but the impact of imposing an AMG-style hierarchy for general sparse matrices remains underexplored.
AI.method: GMP adopts an AMG hierarchy as a structural prior and learns smoothing, restriction, and interpolation operators jointly within a unified GNN framework. It is designed as a drop-in preconditioner for standard Krylov solvers targeting general sparse systems.
AI.result: On a benchmark of over 800 sparse matrices, GMP is compared against classical AMG, single-level ILUT, and state-of-the-art GNN preconditioners. The results characterize regimes where multilevel graph neural preconditioning improves convergence versus where it introduces overhead relative to strong single-level baselines.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight both the promise and the limitations of enforcing AMG-style multilevel structure in learned preconditioners for large-scale scientific simulations, offering guidance on when such approaches are beneficial or detrimental.

title: A log-log upper bound on blow-up rates for the mass-critical half-wave equation

AI.tldr: This paper proves the log-log upper bound for finite-time blow-up in the one-dimensional focusing mass-critical half-wave equation for even initial data with negative energy and mass slightly above ground-state mass, matching the known log-log law for mass-critical NLS.
AI.motivation: To establish the log-log blow-up law for the half-wave equation, analogous to the well-known result for mass-critical nonlinear Schrödinger equations. This is challenging due to the nonlocal operator |D| and the absence of pseudo-conformal symmetry in the half-wave setting.
AI.method: The proof follows the Merle-Raphaël strategy but requires a new blow-up profile construction. This is achieved by combining tail computations carried out to arbitrary order (depending on a dynamical parameter) with Borel integral summation in Λ-analytic spaces, yielding an almost self-similar profile with exponentially small error. The modulation analysis uses a local-virial spectral property proved in a companion paper.
AI.result: The log-log upper bound ||u(t)||_{H^{1/2}} ≲ (log|log(T-t)|/(T-t))^{1/2} as t↑T is established for the half-wave equation with even data, negative energy, and mass slightly above ground-state mass.
AI.conclusion: The half-wave equation exhibits the same log-log blow-up law upper bound as mass-critical NLS, despite the technical difficulties arising from nonlocality and lack of pseudo-conformal symmetry.

title: Discrete to continuum limits in Bayesian inverse problems
summary:
We develop a posterior-level discrete-to-continuum theory for Bayesian inverse problems whose finite-dimensional priors arise from local finite-difference regularization and whose likelihoods are of a general convex GLM-type form. In contrast to continuum-first approaches, the continuum prior and posterior are not assumed at the outset but are constructed as limits of the finite-dimensional probability measures used in numerical computation.
  First, with the total information parameter $τ$ and the regularization strength $κ$ fixed, we prove weak convergence on $L^2$ of the reconstructed discrete Gaussian priors and posterior measures to well-defined continuum laws. We then consider a coupled grid-refinement and small-noise limit in which $N\to\infty$ and $τ_N,κ_N\to\infty$, while $κ_N/τ_N$ remains fixed. Under explicit growth conditions relating $N$ and $τ_N$, we prove that the reconstructed discrete MAP estimates converge to the unique minimizer $u_*$ of the limiting continuum cost functional, that the reconstructed posterior measures concentrate at $u_*$, and that their centered and rescaled fluctuations converge to $\mathcal N(\vec 0,Q^{-1})$, where $Q$ is the Hessian of the continuum cost functional at $u_*$. Finally, we show that the same deterministic limit and Gaussian fluctuation law are obtained by first constructing the continuum posterior and then taking its small-noise, high-regularization limit.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a posterior-level discrete-to-continuum theory for Bayesian inverse problems with local finite-difference regularization priors and general convex GLM-type likelihoods. Rather than assuming continuum priors/postriors upfront, they are constructed as limits of finite-dimensional measures. Under coupled grid-refinement and small-noise limits, discrete MAP estimates converge to the continuum cost minimizer, posterior measures concentrate, and fluctuations converge to a Gaussian law with covariance given by the inverse Hessian of the continuum cost.
AI.motivation: Existing continuum-first approaches assume the continuum prior and posterior from the outset, which may not match what is actually computed numerically from finite-dimensional discretizations. The authors aim to construct a rigorous posterior-level theory that derives continuum objects as genuine limits of the finite-dimensional measures used in computation, ensuring consistency between theory and numerical practice.
AI.method: The paper first fixes the total information parameter τ and regularization strength κ, and proves weak convergence on L² of reconstructed discrete Gaussian priors and posterior measures to well-defined continuum laws. It then considers a coupled limit where grid refinement N→∞ and τ_N, κ_N→∞ with κ_N/τ_N fixed, establishing: (1) convergence of discrete MAP estimates to the unique minimizer of the limiting continuum cost functional under explicit growth conditions on N and τ_N; (2) posterior concentration at the minimizer; (3) convergence of centered/rescaled fluctuations to N(0, Q^{-1}) where Q is the Hessian of the continuum cost at the minimizer.
AI.result: The authors prove that the reconstructed discrete measures converge weakly to continuum laws at fixed parameters, and that in the coupled refinement and small-noise limit, MAP estimates converge, posteriors concentrate, and Gaussian fluctuation limits are obtained. They also demonstrate equivalence: the same deterministic limit and Gaussian fluctuation law arise whether one takes the continuum limit first followed by small-noise/high-regularization limits, or vice versa (commutation of limits).
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a rigorous discrete-to-continuum posterior theory that matches continuum-first approaches in the appropriate asymptotic limits. This validates the consistency between numerical Bayesian computation on finite grids and idealized continuum formulations, showing their results agree in the coupled grid-refinement and small-noise regime.

title: Finite-time blow-up for the mass-critical half-wave equation with negative energy
comment: 121 pages. Computer-assisted verification code, input data, and completed outputs are included as ancillary files and are also available at https://github.com/JeongheonPark-CAP/half-wave-cap-verification
summary:
We study the one-dimensional focusing mass-critical half-wave equation
  \[
  i\partial_tu=|D|u-|u|^2u.
  \]
  For even initial data with negative energy and mass slightly above the ground-state mass, we prove finite-time blow-up and obtain the upper bound \[
  \|u(t)\|_{\dot H^{1/2}}
  \lesssim
  \frac{|\log(T-t)|^{1/4}}{\sqrt{T-t}}
  \qquad\text{as }t\uparrow T. \]
  This is the first finite-time blow-up result for negative-energy solutions to the mass-critical half-wave equation in the near-ground-state regime.
  The proof uses the modulation analysis developed by Merle--Raphaël \cite{MerleRaphael2005AnnMath}. For the half-wave equation, the key missing ingredient is a coercivity estimate for a nonlocal quadratic form generated by the scaling direction. Unlike the local NLS, the half-wave equation does not admit the ODE methods used to establish the corresponding coercivity estimate. Instead, we prove the coercivity estimate by an analytic reduction followed by a rigorous computer-assisted proof.
  The spectral analysis part reduces the coercivity problem to a finite collection of spectral inequalities by combining constrained Morse index arguments with the Birman--Schwinger principle. The computer-assisted part certifies these inequalities by interval arithmetic using a validated approximation of the ground state obtained by compactifying the real line. Together with the modulation analysis, this coercivity theorem gives the finite-time blow-up result.

AI.tldr: The paper proves finite-time blow-up for even, negative-energy, near-ground-state solutions to the one-dimensional focusing mass-critical half-wave equation, establishing an upper blow-up rate bound. The proof combines modulation analysis with a novel coercivity estimate proven via analytic reduction and rigorous computer-assisted verification.
AI.motivation: Establishing the first finite-time blow-up result for negative-energy solutions to the mass-critical half-wave equation in the near-ground-state regime. Unlike the local NLS equation where ODE methods can prove the needed coercivity, the half-wave equation's nonlocal structure requires a fundamentally different approach.
AI.method: The proof uses Merle-Raphael modulation analysis. The key innovation is proving a coercivity estimate for a nonlocal quadratic form via a two-step process: (1) analytic reduction using constrained Morse index arguments and the Birman-Schwinger principle to reduce to finitely many spectral inequalities, and (2) rigorous computer-assisted certification of these inequalities using interval arithmetic with a validated ground-state approximation obtained by compactifying the real line.
AI.result: Proves finite-time blow-up for even initial data with negative energy and mass slightly above ground-state mass, with the upper bound ||u(t)||_{\dot H^{1/2}} ≲ |log(T-t)|^{1/4}/sqrt(T-t) as t↑T. This is the first such finite-time blow-up result for the mass-critical half-wave equation.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes the first finite-time blow-up result for negative-energy solutions to the mass-critical half-wave equation in the near-ground-state regime by overcoming the lack of ODE-based coercivity via a combination of spectral analytic reduction and rigorous computer-assisted verification.

title: Learning features from Newton's algorithm: a way to accelerate nonlinear parametrized PDE solvers
summary: It is well known that Newton's method converges faster when the initial guess is closer to a root of a system of nonlinear equations. In this paper, a two-stage Newton initial guess strategy is proposed by learning features from a parameter-space sampling and a database of precomputed solutions. The method uses discrete Newton trajectories to construct two complementary reduced spaces: a solution feature space, built from converged states, and a corrective search direction feature space, built from intermediate Newton increments. For an unseen parameter, a regression model is used to predict a surrogate solution approximation. Then, in a second step, a residual-minimizing correction is computed using a dedicated GMRES-based approach. The resulting state is then used as an initial guess for the high-fidelity Newton method, which completes convergence. The corrective step is computationally inexpensive since it only requires residual evaluations and the solution of a small least-squares problem. The methodology is weakly intrusive once the high-fidelity residual fields and a script-based programming interface are available. This strategy reduces the number of Newton iterations and decreases the overall CPU time. Numerical experiments on representative PDE problems show quantifiable speedups compared with standalone surrogate initialization. Significant speedups are observed. This generic approach can be applied to a broad class of large-scale nonlinear problems.

AI.tldr: A two-stage Newton initial guess strategy that combines machine learning on precomputed solutions with a GMRES-based residual-minimizing correction to provide high-quality starting points for Newton's method, reducing iterations and CPU time for large-scale nonlinear PDE problems.
AI.motivation: Newton's method converges faster with better initial guesses, but generating high-quality starting points for large-scale nonlinear systems remains challenging. Simply using surrogate-based initialization (e.g., regression from precomputed solutions) is insufficient, motivating a corrective stage to further improve the initial guess quality.
AI.method: Two-stage initial guess strategy: (1) Learn features from parameter-space sampling and precomputed solution database, constructing two complementary reduced spaces—a solution feature space from converged states and a corrective search direction feature space from intermediate Newton increments. (2) For an unseen parameter, use regression to predict a surrogate solution, then apply a residual-minimizing correction via a dedicated GMRES-based approach (requiring only residual evaluations and a small least-squares solve). The corrected state serves as the initial guess for high-fidelity Newton's method.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on representative PDE problems show quantifiable speedups compared to standalone surrogate initialization, with significant reductions in Newton iterations and overall CPU time.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage strategy is a weakly intrusive, generic approach that improves Newton's method efficiency across a broad class of large-scale nonlinear problems.

title: The Follow-the-Leader scheme with non-monotone velocity
summary: This paper addresses the approximation of entropy solutions to a one-dimensional scalar conservation law via the so-called Follow-the-Leader particle scheme in case the velocity map is \emph{non monotone}. The result is based on a discrete maximum principle, on $BV$ estimates of the approximated density, and on the characterization of the limit as entropy solution in the sense of Kru\v zkov.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the Follow-the-Leader particle scheme for approximating entropy solutions of 1D scalar conservation laws with non-monotone velocity maps, proving convergence via discrete maximum principle, BV estimates, and Kružkov entropy characterization.
AI.motivation: Extends the Follow-the-Leader particle scheme analysis from monotone to non-monotone velocity maps, which is a more general and realistic setting for scalar conservation laws.
AI.method: The convergence proof relies on three key ingredients: (1) a discrete maximum principle, (2) BV estimates of the approximated density, and (3) characterization of the limit as an entropy solution in the Kružkov sense.
AI.result: The Follow-the-Leader particle scheme converges to the entropy solution of the scalar conservation law even when the velocity map is non-monotone.
AI.conclusion: The Follow-the-Leader particle scheme is validated as a convergent approximation method for scalar conservation laws with non-monotone velocity maps, broadening its applicability beyond the previously studied monotone case.

title: On Sirakov's equal-frequency uniqueness conjecture
summary:
Let $N\in\{2,3\}$, $0<μ_1\leqμ_2$, and $0<β<μ_1$. We prove that the equal-frequency two-component cubic Schrödinger system \[
  -Δu+u=μ_1u^3+βuv^2,
  \qquad
  -Δv+v=μ_2v^3+βu^2v
  \quad\text{in }\mathbb{R}^N \] has exactly one positive solution in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)\times H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ modulo simultaneous translations. More precisely, every positive solution is a simultaneous translate of the synchronized state constructed from the unique positive radial solution of $-Δw+w=w^3$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$. This settles Sirakov's equal-frequency uniqueness conjecture throughout the weak-coupling range.
  The main difficulty in the proof is to exclude radial solutions for which the ratio of the normalized components is nonconstant. After normalization, the two components satisfy scalar equations with a common potential. We construct a weighted Pohozaev functional for the system together with a correction term and prove that both the corrected functional and the associated weighted functional are strictly positive. Combining these sign properties with a radial flux identity and an auxiliary quotient associated with the component ratio forces synchronization.

AI.tldr: This paper proves the equal-frequency two-component cubic Schrödinger system in R^2 and R^3 has exactly one positive solution modulo translations, settling Sirakov's equal-frequency uniqueness conjecture in the weak-coupling regime.
AI.motivation: To settle Sirakov's equal-frequency uniqueness conjecture for the two-component cubic Schrödinger system in the weak-coupling range, by proving that all positive solutions are synchronized states built from the unique positive radial solution of the scalar equation.
AI.method: The proof excludes nonconstant-component-ratio radial solutions by constructing a weighted Pohozaev functional with a correction term, proving both corrected and weighted functionals are strictly positive, and combining these sign properties with a radial flux identity and an auxiliary quotient to force synchronization.
AI.result: The system has exactly one positive solution in H^1(R^N) x H^1(R^N) modulo simultaneous translations for N=2,3 throughout the weak-coupling range.
AI.conclusion: Sirakov's equal-frequency uniqueness conjecture is settled for the weak-coupling range, confirming that all positive solutions are simultaneous translates of the synchronized state.

title: On boundary regularity for the fractional p-Laplacian with unbounded reactions
summary: We consider an elliptic equation driven by the $s$-fractional $p$-Laplacian, set in a smooth bounded domain $Ω\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ with homogeneous nonlocal Dirichlet conditions and a reaction $f$ lying in $L^q(Ω)$ for some $q\ge 1$. We prove that the unique solution $u$ is $α$-Hölder continuous up to the boundary, for any $α$ below $p'(s-N/pq)$ if $N/ps<q\le N/s$, and $α=s$ if $q>N/s$. Also, we prove that if $q>N/s$ then $u/{\rm d}_Ω^s$ admits a Hölder continuous extension to the closure of $Ω$, where ${\rm d}_Ω$ denotes the distance from the boundary. Our results are almost optimal and extend previous regularity theorems known in the linear case.

AI.tldr: This paper proves optimal Hölder regularity up to the boundary for solutions of the fractional p-Laplace equation with L^q right-hand sides and nonlocal Dirichlet conditions, extending known linear-case results to the nonlinear fractional setting.
AI.motivation: To establish sharp boundary regularity estimates for elliptic equations driven by the s-fractional p-Laplacian with rough (L^q) data, generalizing prior results that were only known in the linear (p=2) case.
AI.method: The authors analyze the regularity of the unique solution u to the fractional p-Laplacian problem. They prove: (i) u is α-Hölder continuous up to the boundary for α below p'(s - N/pq) when N/ps < q ≤ N/s, and α = s when q > N/s; (ii) when q > N/s, the normalized quotient u/d_Ω^s (where d_Ω is the distance-to-boundary function) admits a Hölder continuous extension to the closure of Ω.
AI.result: The paper establishes sharp (almost optimal) boundary Hölder regularity for solutions, with two regimes depending on the integrability q of the reaction term, and proves Hölder continuity of the boundary-normalized quotient u/d_Ω^s in the high-regularity regime. These results extend prior theorems known for the linear case.
AI.conclusion: The regularity results are shown to be almost optimal, and they successfully generalize linear-case boundary regularity theorems to the nonlinear s-fractional p-Laplacian setting with L^q data.

title: Shallow water models for the dynamics of oscillating water columns
summary: We investigate the dynamics of an oscillating water column, which is a wave energy converter where water waves interact with a fixed partially immersed structure and an air chamber. Considering the shallow water regime, the fluid motion is governed by either the one-dimensional nonlinear shallow water equations or the Boussinesq-Abbott equations, while the air pressure variation in the chamber acts as a spring force on the fluid. The presence of the structure and the air chamber introduces constraints into the fluid equations. Assuming conservation of the total fluid-elastic energy in the absence of structural damping, we reformulate the constrained equations as transmission problems between the open water and the chamber and show their local well-posedness. We also consider a different modeling approach in which the upper part of the fluid in the chamber is treated as a rigid layer (water column) free to move vertically above the lower fluid. For this configuration, we reformulate the dynamics as wave-spring-mass systems, where the motion of the water column is driven by the shallow water waves outside the chamber. We establish their local well-posedness and show that the effective buoyancy period of the water column motion is determined by the competition between the added mass and the stiffness of the spring force.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the dynamics of oscillating water columns (OWC) used as wave energy converters, analyzing shallow water wave-chamber interactions through transmission problems and wave-spring-mass system reformulations, proving local well-posedness for both approaches and deriving the effective buoyancy period of the water column.
AI.motivation: To understand and mathematically model the dynamics of oscillating water column wave energy converters, which involve the complex interaction between water waves, a partially immersed structure, and an air chamber, particularly needed for efficient energy conversion and system design.
AI.method: The paper reformulates the constrained shallow water equations (nonlinear shallow water or Boussinesq-Abbott governing equations with air chamber pressure as a spring force) as transmission problems between open water and the chamber, conserving total fluid-elastic energy. It also explores an alternative model treating the upper fluid in the chamber as a rigid water column, reformulated as a wave-spring-mass system.
AI.result: Local well-posedness is established for both modeling approaches (transmission problems and wave-spring-mass systems). The effective buoyancy period of the water column motion is shown to be determined by the competition between added mass and the stiffness of the spring force.
AI.conclusion: Both modeling frameworks provide rigorous mathematical foundations for oscillating water column dynamics in the shallow water regime, with the water column approach revealing that the buoyancy period depends on the balance between added mass effects and spring stiffness.

title: Harmonic, radial, and shell stability of the weighted Einstein constraints on the sphere at infinity
comment: This paper is a companion to version 2 of arXiv:2312.17706 (August 2026). It also incorporates and reorganizes selected material that appeared in version 1 of that paper
summary: We consider fourth-order and second-order partial differential operators localized on domains of the sphere in arbitrary dimension. These operators arise as weighted compositions of the linearized Einstein constraint operators and their adjoints, and played a key role in our resolution of the optimal localization problem in general relativity, also referred to as the gravitational shielding problem. To control the asymptotic behavior of solutions to Einstein's constraints in our companion paper (preprint arXiv:2312.17706), we introduced the notions of harmonic, radial, and shell stability. Harmonic stability controls the borderline harmonic modes, radial stability governs the radial evolution of spherical averages, and shell stability controls the coupled radial-angular evolution of solutions. In the present paper, we establish that these stability properties follow from weighted Poincaré, Korn, and Hardy inequalities. Furthermore, in arbitrary dimension, we investigate the behavior of the associated geometric constants, and conclude that the stability conditions hold for a broad class of localization functions; the theory applies to arbitrarily small localization domains, corresponding to gluing cones with arbitrarily small aperture. At the opposite extreme, our conditions also hold on the entire sphere, corresponding to the absence of localization. This completes, for gluing cones of arbitrarily small aperture in every dimension, the program initiated by A. Carlotto and R. Schoen on gravitational shielding and the construction of solutions enjoying super-harmonic decay estimates. In our proofs, we introduce Hamiltonian and momentum functionals, which we call shell functionals, and show that they enjoy monotonicity and semi-coercivity properties; their structure also suggests possible analogies with functionals arising in other curvature-related geometric problems.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes that harmonic, radial, and shell stability conditions—introduced to control asymptotic behavior of solutions to Einstein's constraint equations—follow from weighted Poincaré, Korn, and Hardy inequalities. The authors analyze the associated geometric constants in arbitrary dimension and show these stability conditions hold for a broad class of localization functions on spheres, ranging from arbitrarily small localization domains (gluing cones with tiny aperture) to the entire sphere (no localization).
AI.motivation: To complete the program initiated by Carlotto and Schoen on gravitational shielding and super-harmonic decay estimates, the authors need to rigorously establish stability conditions for solutions to Einstein's constraints. These stability properties are essential for controlling asymptotic behavior but had not yet been proven to hold generally.
AI.method: The paper proves that harmonic, radial, and shell stability follow from weighted Poincaré, Korn, and Hardy inequalities applied to fourth-order and second-order partial differential operators localized on sphere domains. The authors introduce new "shell functionals" (Hamiltonian and momentum functionals) that possess monotonicity and semi-coercivity properties, and investigate the behavior of associated geometric constants across dimensions.
AI.result: The authors establish that the stability conditions hold for a broad class of localization functions in arbitrary dimension, including the extremes of arbitrarily small localization domains (small-aperture gluing cones) and the full sphere (no localization).
AI.conclusion: This completes the gravitational shielding program for gluing cones of arbitrarily small aperture in every dimension, verifying all necessary stability conditions and extending the theory to its natural domain of validity.

title: Minimal hypersurfaces of Morse index one
summary: We prove that a complete, connected, embedded, minimal hypersurface in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ with finite total curvature and Morse index one is the higher-dimensional catenoid.

AI.tldr: A complete connected embedded minimal hypersurface in R^(n+1) with finite total curvature and Morse index one must be the higher-dimensional catenoid.
AI.motivation: To classify minimal hypersurfaces with specific geometric and spectral constraints (finite total curvature and Morse index one), extending known classification results to higher dimensions.
AI.method: The paper uses the geometric constraints of finite total curvature and Morse index one to prove rigidity, showing that any such hypersurface must be isometric to the higher-dimensional catenoid.
AI.result: The only complete, connected, embedded minimal hypersurface in R^(n+1) with finite total curvature and Morse index one is the higher-dimensional catenoid.
AI.conclusion: This provides a complete classification, confirming the higher-dimensional catenoid as the unique example under these conditions.

title: The stochastic Keller--Segel system in critical spaces
comment: 29 pages. Contribution to the Oberwolfach Report for the Seminar 'Stochastic Partial Differential Equations in Critical Spaces' organized by Antonio Agresti and Mark Veraar
summary:
We study stochastic, parabolic-parabolic Keller--Segel equations on the $d$-dimensional torus in scaling critical Besov spaces, for $d \geq 3$. Using stochastic maximal regularity estimates, we prove local well-posedness of the equation, i.e., that there exists a unique solution up to a maximal time of existence. We show that the time of existence can be made arbitrarily large with arbitrarily high probability, provided that the initial data is sufficiently small in these critical spaces.
  Contribution to the Oberwolfach Report for the Seminar 'Stochastic Partial Differential Equations in Critical Spaces' organized by Antonio Agresti and Mark Veraar.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes stochastic parabolic-parabolic Keller-Segel equations on the d-dimensional torus (d ≥ 3) in scaling critical Besov spaces, proving local well-posedness with unique solutions up to a maximal existence time, and showing that the existence time can be made arbitrarily large with high probability for sufficiently small initial data in these critical spaces.
AI.motivation: The Keller-Segel system models chemotaxis (the directed movement of organisms in response to chemical gradients), and its stochastic version incorporates random perturbations. The authors aim to study this system in scaling critical Besov spaces since d ≥ 3, which presents significant analytical challenges due to the critical scaling regime, extending previous results to the stochastic parabolic-parabolic setting.
AI.method: The authors employ stochastic maximal regularity estimates, a powerful functional analytic tool for handling stochastic PDEs, to establish well-posedness in scaling critical Besov spaces on the d-dimensional torus.
AI.result: They prove local well-posedness, showing the existence of a unique solution up to a maximal time of existence. Additionally, they demonstrate that for sufficiently small initial data in critical Besov spaces, the time of existence can be made arbitrarily large with arbitrarily high probability.
AI.conclusion: The stochastic parabolic-parabolic Keller-Segel system is locally well-posed in scaling critical Besov spaces for d ≥ 3, with a favorable probabilistic long-time existence guarantee for small initial data.

title: Volume Stability for Hyperbolic Manifolds and Applications to General Relativity
summary:
We prove a sharp volume-stability theorem for closed hyperbolic three-manifolds. Let \((M,h)\) be closed hyperbolic with \(\operatorname{Ric}_h=-2h\), and let \(g_i\) be smooth metrics on \(M\) satisfying $R(g_i)\geq -6, \operatorname{Vol}_{g_i}(M)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Vol}_h(M)$. After passing to a subsequence, there exist \(Z_i\subset M\), smooth domains \(K_i\subset M\), and diffeomorphisms $ψ_i:K_i\longrightarrow M\setminus Z_i $
such that $\operatorname{Vol}_{g_i}(Z_i)\longrightarrow0, \operatorname{Vol}_h(M\setminus K_i)\longrightarrow0, $
and $
\|ψ_i^*g_i-h\|_{C^0(K_i,h)}\longrightarrow0. $
Thus near-equality in the sharp hyperbolic volume bound forces tensorial \(C^0\)-convergence to the hyperbolic metric outside regions of vanishing volume. As an application, we establish stability of the Fischer--Moncrief reduced Hamiltonian at the Lorentz-cone ground state: after CMC normalization, near-minimizing compact vacuum data in the hyperbolic topological class converge, modulo sets of vanishing volume, to the hyperbolic Lorentz-cone geometry in tensorial \(C^0\). This provides a rigorous volume-dominance formulation of the Fischer--Moncrief asymptotic picture.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a sharp volume-stability theorem for closed hyperbolic 3-manifolds: if smooth metrics nearly attain the hyperbolic volume lower bound (with scalar curvature R ≥ -6), they must be tensorial C⁰-close to the hyperbolic metric outside sets of vanishing volume. This is applied to establish stability of the Fischer-Moncrief reduced Hamiltonian, showing near-minimizing vacuum data converge to the hyperbolic Lorentz-cone geometry modulo vanishing-volume sets.
AI.motivation: To establish a rigorous volume-dominance formulation of the Fischer-Moncrief asymptotic picture by proving that near-equality in the sharp hyperbolic volume bound forces strong geometric convergence to the hyperbolic metric, connecting scalar curvature rigidity with gravitational Hamiltonian stability.
AI.method: The proof establishes a sharp volume-stability theorem for closed hyperbolic 3-manifolds. Given metrics with R ≥ -6 and volumes converging to the hyperbolic volume, the authors show (after subsequence) existence of vanishing-volume subsets Z_i, large-volume subsets K_i, and diffeomorphisms ψ_i such that the pulled-back metrics converge to the hyperbolic metric in tensorial C⁰ norm on K_i.
AI.result: Near-equality in the sharp hyperbolic volume bound implies tensorial C⁰-convergence to the hyperbolic metric outside regions of vanishing volume. This yields stability of the Fischer-Moncrief reduced Hamiltonian at the Lorentz-cone ground state under CMC normalization.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a rigorous volume-dominance formulation of the Fischer-Moncrief asymptotic picture for compact vacuum data in the hyperbolic topological class, establishing convergence to the hyperbolic Lorentz-cone geometry modulo vanishing-volume sets.

title: On convolved weight matrices and local solvability with controlled loss of regularity
summary: We introduce the convolution between abstractly given anisotropic weight matrices and investigate properties of this new construction. Further, we apply the knowledge to the particular but interesting case when the (isotropic) matrices are associated with weight functions in the sense of Braun-Meise-Taylor and show how the convolution of associated weight matrices modifies the underlying weight functions. Finally, we give a concrete application of the convolution when studying the concept of local solvability for a certain hyperbolic PDE. Indeed, the convolution allows to treat in a natural way a mixed setting; i.e. having a controlled loss of regularity expressed in terms of two, in general different, weight sequences.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a convolution operation for abstractly given anisotropic weight matrices, studies its properties, applies it to weight functions in the Braun-Meise-Taylor sense, and demonstrates a concrete application to local solvability of a hyperbolic PDE with mixed regularity loss expressed via two different weight sequences.
AI.motivation: To develop a mathematical framework for combining anisotropic weight matrices and, more specifically, to enable handling mixed settings where different weight sequences control regularity loss in different directions, particularly relevant for PDE solvability questions.

title: Well-posedness and large deviations for the obstacle problem of first-order stochastic conservation laws
summary: This paper studies the obstacle problem for first-order scalar conservation laws driven by multiplicative noise. By adapting a barrier-substitution strategy to the kinetic formulation, we permit the reflection measure to be a general Radon measure and eliminate the usual obstacle-noise compatibility condition. We establish the existence of kinetic solutions for continuous obstacles and further derive $L^1$-contraction and uniqueness under stronger spatial regularity. Moreover, we prove a Freidlin--Wentzell large deviation principle in $L^1(0,T;L^1(\mathbb{T}^N))$. Unlike existing large-deviation arguments based on control-uniform penalization of the obstacle, we work directly with the reflected skeleton equation and retain the possibly singular Radon reflection measure throughout, while a viscous approximation provides the spatial $H^1$-regularity required for compactness before passing to the inviscid limit. Our results provide a hyperbolic counterpart to the large deviation theory for parabolic reflected SPDEs developed by Matoussi, Sabbagh, and Zhang (2021).

title: Reflected diffusion, no-flux continuity equations and confined Lagrangian flows in bounded domains
summary: Motivated by marginal distribution flows of reflected diffusions in bounded domains, we investigate when a density/flux pair solving a no-flux continuity equation admits a regular Lagrangian flow that remains in the closed domain and generates the prescribed density flow. We give sufficient conditions in terms of interior bounded-variation regularity, bounded-variation control on a boundary collar, a one-sided bound on an absolutely continuous divergence, and vanishing normal trace of the velocity. The proof uses the fact that tangency removes the singular boundary contribution to the divergence of the zero extension, thereby making the extended velocity admissible for the Ambrosio-DiPerna-Lions theory. We show that these boundary assumptions cannot be jointly relaxed so as to admit a boundary current mechanism. We construct an explicit smooth density/flux pair carrying a boundary current. Its density evolution is unique in a weighted class and its characteristics are unique, confined and transport the marginals, yet it admits no regular Lagrangian flow because the compressibility bound fails arbitrarily close to the initial time. We also establish two uniqueness results for no-flux Fokker-Planck equations: a duality result for bounded measurable drifts and a weighted energy result for entrance-type drifts singular at the boundary. Our results provide a rigorous mathematical justification for using the ODE-based sampling of reflected diffusion models under minimal regularity assumptions on the coefficients, and also indicate when such ODE-based samplers may fail.

It also proves uniqueness results for no-flux Fokker-Planck equations and justifies ODE-based sampling of reflected diffusions under minimal regularity assumptions.
